bio.en: Todd Jackson is a partner at First Round Capital and a rare VC who came up as a product leader - PM of Gmail, Facebook News Feed/Photos/Groups, Twitter product director, Dropbox VP of product & design, and a founder.
bio.zh: Todd Jackson 是 First Round Capital 的合伙人，也是一位罕见的、从产品领导者成长起来的投资人——他曾任 Gmail 产品经理、Facebook 动态消息/照片/小组产品负责人、Twitter 产品总监、Dropbox 产品与设计副总裁，同时也是一位创始人。

summary.en: Todd shares how a product leader thinks as a VC, including what he looks for in founders and teams, and how his operating background shapes his investments. He discusses lessons from building Gmail, the Facebook News Feed redesign, and Dropbox, plus why he believes more operators should move into venture. The episode is a unique blend of product craft and investing wisdom.
summary.zh: Todd 分享了一位产品领导者作为投资人是如何思考的，包括他在创始人与团队身上寻找什么，以及他的运营背景如何塑造其投资。他讨论了打造 Gmail、Facebook 动态消息改版与 Dropbox 的经验，以及为什么他认为更多运营者应当进入风投。本期是产品手艺与投资智慧的独特融合。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Finding product-market fit is the single most important thing that your startup does in the first three years, and it's just underexplored and it's just underexplained as a topic.
turns.zh: 找到产品与市场的契合点，是创业公司在前三年最重要的工作。但这个话题却鲜少被深入探讨和清晰解析。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been working on a product-market fit framework.
turns.zh: 你一直在致力于打造产品与市场的契合框架。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: We've published dozens of articles on the First Round Review, and we have found a very consistent set of patterns, demand satisfaction, and efficiency. But the interesting thing is that you don't go for all three of them from the very beginning.
turns.zh: 我们在《First Round Review》上发表了数十篇相关文章，发现了一套非常一致的模式——满足需求、提升效率。但有趣的是，并非所有公司一开始就能同时做到这三点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's essentially four levels of product-market fit: nascent, developing, strong, extreme.
turns.zh: 产品与市场的契合度本质上分为四个层次：萌芽、发展、强化、极致。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Roughly, 60% are never going to get past L2.
turns.zh: 大约60%的公司永远无法突破L2阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These four Ps is essentially what you should try to change if you're stuck.
turns.zh: 如果你陷入困境，应该重点调整以下四个核心要素。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: You've got the persona, the problem, the promise, and the product. Lattice kept the first one but changed the others. Vanta changed all four.
turns.zh: 包括目标用户、核心问题、价值主张和产品本身。Lattice保留了目标用户，但调整了其他要素；Vanta则全面革新了全部四个维度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hearing level three tells me level two is basically your pivot from: I'm just grinding, selling, pitching.
turns.zh: 当你听到第三层级时，这意味着你已从最初的埋头苦干、销售推广和推销演示阶段，成功完成了二级转变。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: This is where it starts to get fun.
turns.zh: 这才是真正激动人心的时刻。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Lenny, I'm excited to be here. Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 莱尼，我很高兴能来参加这次访谈。感谢你们邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So first of all, just to mention you're a VC, which is very rare for this podcast. But you're a very special VC, you have a deep background in product, and I thought it might be helpful just to give a little bit of context on your product background, your product bona fides so people will get a real sense of just how legit you are as a product thinker.
turns.zh: 首先，得提一下你是一位风险投资人（VC），这在我们的播客中实属罕见。但你是一位非常特别的VC，你在产品领域有着深厚的背景。我觉得先简要介绍一下你的产品背景和资历，或许能让听众更清楚你作为产品思考者的专业度。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah, you got it. So I am a VC. I'm a partner at First Round Capital now, and I've been at First Round for four years. But I was not a VC before First Round. So I started a company in 2013 called Cover, and that was actually funded by First Round 11 years ago. That's how I got to know First Round. And before that, I had worked on Gmail as the product lead in the early days, early 2000s and at Facebook. (00:05:39): And then I started Cover, and we ended up selling Cover to Twitter in 2014. And I worked on a bunch of different products at Twitter. And then I was the VP of product and design at Dropbox. That was 2015 to 2018. So I have always loved product, and that's actually the reason now that I love being a seed stage VC because I love investing at the early stage founders who are pre-product-market fit and then helping them get there. And I just love doing that over and over again.
turns.zh: 没错，你说得对。我现在是First Round Capital的合伙人，已经在First Round工作了四年。但在加入First Round之前，我并非传统意义上的VC。2013年，我创办了一家名为Cover的公司，11年前它就获得了First Round的投资，这也是我与First Round结缘的契机。在此之前，我曾在2000年代初参与Gmail的产品开发，并在Facebook任职。（00:05:39）随后，我创办了Cover，并于2014年将其出售给Twitter。此后，我在Twitter负责过多个产品项目。2015至2018年间，我还担任Dropbox的产品与设计副总裁。一直以来，我都热爱产品设计工作，这也正是如今我热衷于担任种子期VC的原因——我喜欢投资那些尚未实现产品市场匹配的初创公司，并助力他们达成这一目标。这种循环往复的过程让我乐在其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like we could have a whole other podcast episode on why you decided to move into venture versus staying in product.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们完全可以单独做一期播客，探讨你为何选择投身风险投资而非继续深耕产品领域。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: We can do it.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But we're going to stay focused. So the reason we're here is that for over a year, you've been working on a product-market fit framework, essentially, a framework to help founders and product teams find product-market fit, which we should talk about this. But this is the most important thing you've got to get right as a founder in a product team is finding product-market fit. I got a peek at this framework. I love it. I love the way you've structured it, the way you're thinking about it. (00:06:36): So what we're going to do today is walk through this framework in depth. First, I just want to spend a few minutes on setting a little context just so people understand who this is for and how to think about this. So maybe a first question is just why do you believe people need a framework for finding product-market fit? And just also, if you want to touch on why is product-market fit so important? Why is that something people should even be thinking about?
turns.zh: 不过今天我们还是要专注正题。过去一年多来，你一直在研发产品市场匹配框架，旨在帮助创业者和产品团队找到产品市场匹配点，这正是我们今天要深入探讨的核心话题。但对创业者和产品团队而言，产品市场匹配是至关重要的环节。我曾了解过这个框架，深感赞赏——你构建框架的方式以及思路都令人惊叹。（00:06:36）今天我们将深入解析这个框架。首先，我想花几分钟时间做个背景介绍，让听众明白这个框架的适用对象，以及如何理解其核心逻辑。或许可以先从一个问题入手：为何你认为人们需要一个产品市场匹配框架？再者，产品市场匹配为何如此重要？为何这是创业者和产品团队必须关注的核心要素？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: The thing about product-market fit is that I find it's mysterious to a lot of people, and people tend to think about it purely as an art rather than a science. And all the advice that you find out there on the internet is very general when it comes to product-market fit. You'll know it when you see it, you'll know it when you have it. It's not specific. And there's so many other startup topics where there is good content on the internet like hiring your first salesperson, running board meetings, stuff that is specific and tactical. But there isn't that much content around product-market fit that is that specific. (00:07:33): And so I think that's actually why Rahul from Superhuman is well-known for his approach to finding product-market fit. That was published on the First Round Review in 2018, and it was immediately popular and interesting to people. And I think the reason is because it was specific and because it was tactical and it brought a little bit of the science to something that people thought was just an art. And I think it's why your content is really popular too, Lenny. (00:07:57): You and I worked on this product validation article together a little while back, and the seven part series that you did on B2B SaaS companies and the PMF benchmarking data that you had, I think it was how long it took to get to a product and a customer and to product-market fit, that was super well-read. And there just isn't that much good specific content about this. But like you said, product-market fit is the single most important thing that your startup does in the first three years and it's just underexplored, it's underexplained as a topic. (00:08:28): So we felt this was a very important thing to do, something worth focusing on. And I've personally talked to hundreds of founders about this topic. We've published dozens of articles on the First Round Review. We call this our Paths to Product-Market Fit Series where we interview founders about the early days. And I'm just always interested in what are the patterns. If you talk to enough successful founders, and in this case, it can be enterprise founders, and you ask them, "What did you do in the first six to nine months of running your company, of starting your company? What patterns emerged from that?" And we have found a very consistent set of patterns, and that's what we decided to base our framework around.
turns.zh: 关于产品市场契合度（product-market fit），我发现很多人对它感到神秘，人们往往把它视为一门艺术而非科学。网上关于产品市场契合度的建议通常都很笼统，比如“你看到它时就知道了，拥有它时你也会知道”。但这些建议缺乏具体指导。相比之下，其他创业主题如招聘首位销售人员、召开董事会会议等，就有许多具体实用的内容。但关于产品市场契合度的专业指导却少之又少。（00:07:33）所以我认为这正是Superhuman的拉胡尔（Rahul）因其产品市场契合度方法而闻名的原因。他在2018年在First Round Review上发表的文章，立即受到人们的欢迎和关注。我认为原因在于他的方法具体、实用，将人们认为纯粹是艺术的东西注入了科学性。（00:07:57）伦尼（Lenny），你和我不久前一起撰写了产品验证文章。你关于B2B SaaS公司和产品市场契合度基准数据的七部分系列文章，特别是关于产品、客户和产品市场契合度所需时间的研究，读者反响热烈。但关于这一主题的优质具体内容实在太少了。正如你所说，产品市场契合度是创业公司前三年最重要的事情，但作为一个主题却被严重忽视和误解。（00:08:28）因此，我们认为这是一个非常重要且值得关注的课题。我个人与数百位创始人讨论过这个话题。在First Round Review上发表了数十篇文章。我们将其命名为“产品市场契合度之路”系列，采访初创公司的创始人。我们始终对其中的模式感兴趣。如果你与足够成功的创始人交流（在这种情况下，可以是企业创始人），并询问他们：“在公司运营的头六到九个月里，你们做了什么？出现了哪些模式？”我们发现了一套非常一致的模式，这也正是我们构建框架的基础。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And I think you're at such an interesting Venn diagram of exposure to develop something like this. One, you have a deep product background, you started a company, you see tons of startups going through the journey, many succeeding, many not. So I get why one, you wanted to do this and why I think this is going to be so valuable to a lot of people. You talked briefly about why product-market fit is so important, and maybe it might be helpful just to share a little bit more just why is this something people should be so obsessed with and why did you spend so much time developing this?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我认为你有非常独特的背景和经验来开发这样的内容。一方面，你有深厚的产品背景，创办过公司，见证了无数初创公司的兴衰。因此我理解你为何想做这件事，也明白这对很多人会非常有价值。你简要谈到了产品市场契合度为何如此重要，或许可以再多分享一些，让人们更清楚为什么要如此执着于它，以及你为何投入大量时间研发这个框架？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think as a founder, there are so many things you have to do. You have to pick a market, you have to find a co-founder, you have to hire a team, you have to raise funding, you have to build a product, you have to sell a product. And so sometimes it gets lost that actually, the only thing that matters in the first couple years is finding product-market fit and actually, what we define as extreme product-market fit, and I'll go into that. Because if you find extreme product-market fit, the momentum just carries you, and the market pulls you along. And it's easy to know what to build because you're building the thing that your customers want and it's motivating as a team. It's easy to hire people, everything becomes easier if you find product-market fit, it is the thing that propels the company. (00:10:25): And so we are a seed stage venture firm. We tend to work with very early founders who are pre-product-market fit. And the hard truth about it is that most of them don't get past the first couple levels of it. The majority of startups do not get past, what we call, level one product-market fit or level two product-market fit. And I'll go through and define all that stuff. They get stuck at one of those first couple levels. And if they can unlock the right product and the right way to explain it to a customer and make a customer deeply satisfied, and there's enough customers out there like that, it just pulls the whole thing along.
turns.zh:
我认为，作为一名创业者，需要做的事情太多了。你得选定市场、寻找联合创始人、组建团队、筹集资金、开发产品、销售产品。有时人们会忽略，在创业的头几年里，真正重要的是找到产品与市场的契合点——也就是我们所说的极致的产品与市场契合点。我稍后会详细解释这个概念。因为一旦找到极致的产品与市场契合点，势头就会顺势而为，市场也会推动你前进。这样一来，你就能轻松判断该开发什么产品，因为你开发的正是客户真正需要的东西，这对团队来说也极具激励性。招聘人才也会变得容易许多——只要找到契合点，一切都会迎刃而解，产品与市场的契合点就是企业的驱动力。

（00:10:25）我们是一家种子期风险投资公司。我们倾向于与那些尚未找到产品与市场契合点的早期创业者合作。残酷的事实是，大多数创业者都无法突破前两个阶段。我们所说的第一级产品与市场契合点或第二级产品与市场契合点，是大多数创业者无法跨越的障碍。我会详细解释这些概念。他们往往卡在前两个阶段的某个关卡。如果能找到正确的产品，找到合适的方式向客户解释，让客户深感满意，并且有足够多这样的客户支持，那么整个局面就会水到渠成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who is this framework for specifically? And for people that are listening, how do they know if this is for them or not?
turns.zh: 这个框架具体针对谁？对于听众来说，如何判断这是否适合他们？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: This is for early B2B founders, and specifically founders who are doing something that is more sales-led than bottom-up. I think bottom-up is its own world. It's closer to consumer product development in my mind. And I have done consumer products. Consumer product, I think there is a little bit more alchemy involved. It's about having great taste and finding the right thing at the right time and it's like catching lightning in a bottle. (00:11:36): I think the good thing about enterprise, and specifically sales-led B2B, is that there is more science to it. And so it is for sales-led B2B founders who are in, let's call it, the first six to nine months of starting their company and want to set the foundation for product-market fit right from the beginning.
turns.zh:
这个框架专为B2B领域的早期创业者设计，特别是那些以销售为导向而非自下而上开发产品的人。我认为自下而上的模式自成一派。在我看来，它更接近消费品开发。我自己也做过消费品业务。在我看来，消费品开发需要更多的“魔法”——要具备敏锐的洞察力，能在正确的时间找到正确的产品，简直是天作之合。

（00:11:36）我认为B2B领域，尤其是以销售为导向的B2B创业者，存在更科学的逻辑。因此，这个框架适合那些在创业初期（比如创立公司后的前六到九个月）就想从一开始就为产品与市场契合点奠定基础的创业者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So B2B founders, sales-led in the first six to nine months of their journey. Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。所以B2B领域的创业者，在创业旅程的头六到九个月里，销售导向型的。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: That's right. Yes.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about the science of this. I imagine you don't want to overpromise this is going to help you find product-market fit, step one, two, three profit. How do you think about just what the benefits of this are and how people should think about the chance that they will find product-market fit at the end of this journey following this framework?
turns.zh: 你提到这里面有科学依据。我想你不会夸大其词，声称这个框架能帮助他们找到产品与市场的契合点，第一步、第二步、第三步就能盈利。你如何看待其中的好处，以及人们应该如何看待遵循这个框架后最终找到产品与市场契合点的可能性？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: We can't guarantee success here. I just want to contextualize that finding extreme product-market fit is very, very hard. And what we are trying to do is increase your odds, increase the odds, reduce the role of luck, give you a framework and way of thinking about the things that you need to do. And I think that that can increase the odds. Like I said earlier, the majority of startups are getting stuck at these first couple levels. I think if you know what the path looks like and you know what the levers are at your disposal and you know what you need to aim for, I think we can get more of these companies to level three and level four product-market fit, which is where you really want to be and where you have a very valuable company.
turns.zh: 我们无法保证在这里取得成功。我只想说明，找到极致的产品-市场契合度是极其困难的。我们试图做的是提高你们成功的概率，降低运气因素的影响，为你们提供一个框架和思考路径，帮助你们明确需要达成的目标。我认为这样能显著提升成功几率。正如我之前所说，大多数初创公司都卡在前几个阶段。如果你清楚前进的路径、掌握可用的资源、明确目标方向，我相信我们能帮助更多公司突破第三、第四阶段的产品-市场契合度关卡——这才是你真正渴望达到的境界，也是打造极具价值的企业的关键阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. Okay, final question. You launched a whole program for founders to go through and learn all of this in depth, many week kind of program. We're going to be covering a lot of it here for folks that want to go a lot deeper and actually go through this program. Talk about how they find this and how this program works.
turns.zh: 好。最后一个问题，你们推出了一个完整的项目，帮助创业者深入学习这些内容。这是一个为期数周的深度项目。我们会为那些希望深入探索并参与该项目的人详细解析。请谈谈如何找到这个项目，以及项目的运作方式。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So we launched a new program, and we call it Product-Market Fit Method. It is designed, like I said, to help early B2B founders increase the odds of finding product-market fit. It's totally free, it's a very intensive program. You can see all the details at pmf.firstround.com, and the application deadline is May 7th. The program starts on May 29th. And we actually ran a beta version, a test version of this late last year with 11 founders, I think probably some you know, Lenny, from Stripe and Plaid and Airbnb and Twitter. And the feedback, it was great. It made me feel very good. (00:13:47): One of the founders was like, "I feel like these 14 weeks saved me two years of time in what would've been wandering through the desert." And so there's eight sessions in the full program, and the first one is the one we're going to do today. So the first session is on what we call the levels of product-market fit. The second one is on customer discovery, and we actually refer to it as dollar-driven discovery. We get very specific about not just the normal way of doing customer conversations and customer discovery, but how do you find that a customer is willing to pay money for this thing and a lot of money? (00:14:22): We talk about market validation, product positioning. We do a section on design partners because I think a lot of founders have questions about that. How do I find the right design partners? What's the right way to structure an agreement with them? How do I convert them to paying customers? All that stuff. We talk about product iteration and pivots, and I refer to this stage as the grind, the grind of product iteration. And then we spend a ton of time on founder-led sales. (00:14:47): And the reason that we do that is we really like working with very technical founders, builders, people that are either engineering background, product design, data science, people who are builders. So that's the program in a nutshell. And like I said, any founder working on a new B2B SaaS company, welcome to apply. And then bonus points if you are technical, like I said, if you have a clear product idea or a hypothesis, but that you're less than six to 12 months into building the company.
turns.zh: 我们推出了一个新项目，名为"产品-市场契合度方法"。正如我之前所说，该项目旨在帮助早期B2B创业者提高找到产品-市场契合度的成功概率。项目完全免费，课程强度很大。详情请访问pmf.firstround.com，申请截止日期为5月7日，项目将于5月29日正式启动。去年底我们曾为11位创业者试运行过测试版，其中不乏业界知名人士，如Stripe、Plaid、Airbnb和Twitter的创始人。反馈非常积极，让我倍感欣慰。（00:13:47）一位创业者感慨道："这14周的课程为我节省了两年时间，让我在迷茫中找到了方向。"完整项目共八个阶段，首节课即今日的"产品-市场契合度阶段"。第二节课聚焦客户发现，我们称之为"美元驱动的发现"。我们不仅深入探讨常规的客户对话与客户发现方法，更重点解析如何判断客户愿意为产品付费，甚至支付高额费用。（00:14:22）我们讲解市场验证、产品定位，特别关注设计伙伴选择，解答诸多创业者疑惑：如何找到合适的设计伙伴？如何构建合作协议？如何将其转化为付费客户？我们还深入探讨产品迭代与转型，将这一阶段称为"产品迭代的煎熬期"。最后我们重点讲解创始人主导的销售策略。（00:14:47）之所以设计这些模块，是因为我们乐于与技术型创业者合作——无论是工程师背景、产品设计、数据科学等技术领域。总之，这个项目就是为技术型创业者量身打造的。欢迎所有从事B2B SaaS新项目的创业者申请参与。若你具备技术背景、清晰的产品构想或假设，且公司成立时间不足6至12个月，优先考虑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how incentives are so aligned here. You help companies find product-market fit. If First Round does great, everyone does great. It makes so much sense to build something like this. One thing I can't help but mention or ask about is you said it's an intensive program. How do you find founders have time to do something like this and also be building their company? I know this helps them build, but how do you just think about they have so much to do, they have time to do a program like this?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这里激励机制的深度契合。你帮助公司找到产品与市场的完美匹配。如果First Round做得出色，每个人都会受益。打造这样一个平台实在是明智之举。但我不禁要提及或追问一点——你说这是一个密集型项目。创始人们如何能抽出时间参与，又能同时专注于公司发展？我知道这能助力他们成长，但面对繁重的工作任务，他们怎么还能抽出时间参与这个项目？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: The way that we think about it is that the program roughly takes about 10 hours a week for each founder, and it's 10 hours of work that you were going to be doing anyway. It is literally you're talking to customers, you're improving your positioning, you're doing critical thinking about your market and what you should be building. And so the way I think about it, and the way I've heard from the 11 founders that went through it is it just added structure to what I was doing anyway and it actually made me more efficient.
turns.zh: 我们的思路是，这个项目每位创始人每周大约需要投入10小时，而这些时间原本也是他们需要完成的工作。这段时间里，他们会与客户沟通，优化产品定位，深入思考市场需求和产品方向。在我看来，对于参与过项目的11位创始人而言，这个项目为他们现有的工作注入了结构化思维，实际上提高了他们的工作效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question, you mentioned that it's free. How does that work? How does that work for everyone?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你提到这个项目是免费的。具体如何运作？对所有参与者都是免费的吗？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So it's 100% free and literally, it costs you $0. We give you $0, we own 0% of your company. And it's pretty different than I think a lot of other programs out there. And this is just something we do. Over the years, we've run First Round Angel Track, which I know you were in, Lenny. We've run the First Round Review for 10 years. We make these things free and our belief is that you have to create value in the ecosystem. (00:16:36): You have to put stuff out in the world that is useful, and if you can create that value, create enough value with the audience, then you'll be able to capture that value at some point. And so we think there's a win-win here. We get an inside look at some of tomorrow's great companies and they get an inside look at First Round.
turns.zh: 完全免费，零成本。我们不收取任何费用，也不持有公司股份。这与其他类似项目有很大不同。这是我们秉持的理念。多年来，我们举办了First Round Angel Track（天使导师计划），我知道你也参与过这个项目。First Round Review（评审计划）我们也开展了10年。我们将这些项目免费开放，因为我们坚信要为生态系统创造价值。（00:16:36）：你需要输出有价值的内容，如果能为受众创造足够的价值，最终就能从中获益。我们认为这是一个双赢局面。我们能提前洞察未来优秀公司的潜力，他们也能深入了解First Round的运作模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So companies don't have to take money from you guys to be a part of this program.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以参与这个项目的公司无需向你们融资？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's get into it. Let's talk about this framework. Maybe just as a broad strokes overview, how does this framework work? How do companies find product-market fit?
turns.zh: 好的，让我们深入探讨这个框架。或许先从宏观视角概述一下，这个框架是如何运作的？公司如何找到产品与市场的完美契合点？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So the framework starts with a very simple idea that is product-market fit is not a one-size-fits-all thing, and it doesn't just happen overnight. And for B2B companies, specifically, it does tend to follow a repeatable pattern. And so we start with defining the ultimate goal. The ultimate goal is to get to extreme product-market fit. And we have a precise definition for this. Let me read it to you. So extreme product-market fit is a state of widespread demand for a product that satisfies a critical need and crucially can be delivered repeatably and efficiently to each customer. (00:17:40): And so there's three key ideas in there: demand, satisfaction and efficiency. And I think efficiency is worth highlighting because that's what most people would leave out of their definition. You talk about like, "Oh, it's a product, people like it. That's good, that's product-market fit." But if you look, there's products out there. I was a big fan of WeWork, as a customer of WeWork. And I'm a fan of Casper and these other products. Those products managed to achieve customer satisfaction and demand, but they never got the efficiency right, and so the whole business just never worked at scale. (00:18:18): And my partner, Brett Berson, at First Round, he gives this example of the $100 vending machine, and I really like this example, which is imagine I built a vending machine and I stuck it in the middle of San Francisco. And you walk up to this vending machine and you put a dollar in and $100 bill comes out. And that's the product. That would have insane demand. There would be a line at that vending machine. I think people would be extremely satisfied. They'd be like, "This is awesome." The retention would be very good. I'm sure they would come back tomorrow. But the whole thing is it's ridiculous. The whole metaphor is ridiculous because it's just not viable to do something like that. (00:18:59): And yet you see a lot of startups kind of do this. They're basically with their products, giving away $2 for $1 and it gets them pretty far. But that's not real product-market fit. And so that's one of the reasons that we think efficiency and how you think about the economic model of what you're doing is very important. And then this other aspect that I like, which is we have this concept that we call the marginal customer, and the next incremental customer you're going to get for your company, for your product. And if you have product-market fit, and as you are progressing along this journey, the marginal customer should be getting easier and easier and easier to get, easier to acquire them, easier to give them good service with a good product. (00:19:42): And that means your efficiency is increasing along the way and your product-market fit is strengthening. So you've got to have all three of those things: demand, satisfaction, efficiency. But the interesting thing is that you don't go for all three of them at once from the very beginning. And so product-market fit, it happens in the sequence of levels, it happens over multiple years. And for the best enterprise companies, I would say they tend to reach extreme product-market fit in roughly four to six years. There's some variance, but roughly four to six years. And so we label these four levels. We say level one product-market fit is nascent product-market fit. Level two is developing, level three is strong, and level four is extreme. And that's where you want to get. (00:20:26): And along the way, you're trading off these three dimensions: satisfaction, demand, and efficiency because they're intertwined. You could spend a bunch of money on marketing, and that's going to increase your demand, but you're decreasing your efficiency if you do that. You can invest a bunch in efficiency and automating a whole bunch of stuff, but that actually might harm the customer experience and you're reducing satisfaction. So that's an interesting thing, I think, is you're actually making trade-offs at each level and what you should optimize for at each level is different. And so we talk about all these signs, whether you're getting stuck at a given level, how do you get unstuck and how do you progress along this path.
turns.zh:
因此，这个框架始于一个非常简单的观点：产品与市场的契合并非千篇一律，也不是一蹴而就的。对于B2B公司而言，这种契合往往遵循可重复的模式。我们首先要明确最终目标——实现极致的产品与市场契合。为此，我们给出了一个精确的定义。让我为大家解读一下。极致的产品与市场契合是指产品满足关键需求、广泛被市场接受，并且能够高效且可重复地为每位客户提供服务的状态。（00:17:40）这里有三个关键要素：需求、满足度和效率。我认为效率这一点值得强调，因为这是大多数人在定义产品与市场契合时容易忽略的部分。人们常说：“产品不错，用户喜欢，这就是契合了。” 但仔细观察市场，你会发现有些产品虽然满足了用户需求和满足感，但始终无法实现高效运营，最终无法形成规模化商业模式。（00:18:18）First Round的合伙人Brett Berson举了一个例子：100美元自动售货机。我很喜欢这个比喻——假设你把一台自动售货机放在旧金山市中心，用户投入一美元就能获得100美元现金。这就是极致的产品。但现实中，这样的方案根本不可行，因为它缺乏经济可行性。

（00:18:59）然而许多初创公司却在效仿这种模式。他们通过1美元换2美元的策略勉强维持，但这并非真正的产品与市场契合。因此，效率和商业模式的可行性至关重要。另一个关键概念是“边际客户”。边际客户是指你为公司或产品争取的下一个增量用户。若产品与市场契合良好，随着业务发展边际客户获取难度会逐渐降低。（00:19:42）这意味着效率提升和契合度增强是相辅相成的。要实现极致的产品与市场契合，必须同时满足需求、满足度和效率三个要素。但关键在于并非一开始就同时达标，而是分阶段演进。优秀的企业级公司通常在4到6年内实现极致契合，具体时长存在差异，但大致在此区间。我们将契合度分为四个阶段：初级阶段、发展阶段、强化阶段和极致阶段。（00:20:26）在过程中，我们需要平衡三个维度：满足度、需求和效率，因为它们是相互关联的。
两者相互交织。你可以投入大量资金用于营销，这会增加需求，但同时也会降低效率。同样，你也可以在提升效率和实现大量自动化方面投入大量资源，但这可能会损害客户体验，降低客户满意度。所以我认为一个很有意思的点是，在每个层级上你都需要进行权衡，而每个层级的优化重点也各不相同。因此，我们会探讨各种迹象，比如当你卡在某个层级时该如何突破，以及如何沿着这条路径不断前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And we're going to go through each of these. And the idea, as a listener, what I'm thinking is you're probably in one of these buckets. What we're trying to do is help you out of that bucket and help you move further up the ladder to the next level. So just to summarize, I have my notes here. So there's essentially four levels of product-market fit, basically, the strength of product-market fit that you have: nascent, developing, strong, extreme.
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来我们要逐一分析这些阶段。作为听众，我觉得你们可能正处于其中某个阶段。我们要做的就是帮助你们跳出这个阶段，朝着更高层次的目标迈进。简单总结一下，我这里有笔记。产品与市场匹配度的四个阶段基本对应着匹配度的强弱：萌芽阶段、发展阶段、强势阶段和极致阶段。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then you have three dimensions within each of these levels: satisfaction, demand, and efficiency. We're going to talk about what all these mean and how you use these. Let's talk about level one, nascent product-market fit. What does that look like? What do you do when you're there if you're stuck? And what are some examples of companies that felt nascent product-market fit?
turns.zh: 好的。每个阶段又有三个维度：满意度、需求和效率。我们来详细讲解每个维度的含义及应用方式。先从第一阶段——萌芽阶段说起。它是什么样的？如果卡在这一阶段该怎么办？有没有典型的案例？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, level one, nascent. So at this point, you're probably like a pre-seed or seed stage company. You've got less than 10 people on your team. And at level one, your job is to find three to five customers that have a particular problem that is worth solving and to deliver them a satisfying solution. And you got to pick a problem that is both important and urgent to them. (00:22:08): And the solution that you deliver needs to satisfy some kind of promise that they care deeply about. So of the three dimensions that you just recapped, Lenny, it's satisfaction first, demand second, efficiency last when you're at level one. It's actually okay to be inefficient at this stage if it helps you uncover something that delivers an insanely good customer satisfaction. And so I think that one of the best examples I can think of that is this company called Vanta.
turns.zh: 是的。第一阶段是萌芽阶段。这时候你可能处于种子期或早期阶段，团队规模不到10人。第一阶段的核心任务是找到3到5个客户，他们有值得解决的具体问题，并为他们提供令人满意的解决方案。要选择对他们既重要又紧迫的问题。提供的解决方案必须满足他们高度关注的某项承诺。（00:22:08）在第一阶段，效率可以先放一放，但要确保能发现能带来极致客户满意度的关键点。我能想到的最佳案例之一是Vanta公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love Vanta. Also, a happy sponsor and I'm an investor. What a great example.
turns.zh: 我超爱Vanta。他们也是我的投资对象，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: What a great example. So Vanta was founded in 2016 by Christina Cacioppo, and she had come from Dropbox and we got to work at Dropbox together, which was awesome. She was the PM of Dropbox Paper at that time. And so Vanta, it's a company that does compliance automation, continuous monitoring. And most startups think of Vanta is how you get a SOC 2, but they didn't do that at first. (00:23:03): And I remember in 2018, Christina and I went on a walk around the South Park neighborhood in San Francisco. And this was the first time I heard the idea of Vanta. And she had actually, in 2016, 2017, tried a few other ideas. She had this smart speaker that would record meetings and it would send meeting summaries over Slack.
turns.zh: 确实很棒。Vanta由Christina Cacioppo于2016年创立，她之前在Dropbox工作，曾与我共事过。她当时是Dropbox Paper的产品经理。Vanta专注于合规自动化和持续监控。大多数初创公司认为Vanta是获取SOC 2认证的工具，但他们最初并没有走这条路。（00:23:03）记得2018年，我和Christina在旧金山南公园附近散步时，她第一次向我提起Vanta的创意。2016、2017年她尝试过其他方向，比如智能音箱录制会议并通过Slack发送会议摘要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: B2B Alexa is what she called it. I remember.
turns.zh: 她称之为B2B版的Alexa。我记得的。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: B2B Alexa. And she had this other idea, something about dropshipping, but she didn't know anything about dropshipping. And she had just been in this mode of like, "We're building stuff and then we're seeing if anybody wants it." And then she realized that wasn't working and she changed what she was doing. And she started talking to potential customers, and she was very interested in the idea of security and why a lot of startups didn't use any security products. (00:23:48): And she was talking to security engineers and CISOs and just CTOs and startups. And she would ask them, "What is the thing you hate most about your job as it relates to security?" And over and over and over they would say, "I hate filling out the security questionnaires. I hate doing the compliance audits. It's so much grungy manual work. I'm in there filling out spreadsheets and taking screenshots of my AWS account. And the whole thing just doesn't make sense." And she had actually felt this herself when she was on Dropbox Paper and the experience of getting a SOC 2 was onerous. (00:24:26): And the reason that she needed to get it is because we wanted to start selling Dropbox Paper into enterprise. And so she said to me, "There's this pain out there, I think I can solve it, and I think there might be a revenue unlock." And I was like, "What do you mean by that?" And she was like, "Well, I've got these first few customers or design partner, pseudo customers. It's Segment and Front and Figma." And this is 2017, '18. So these companies were smaller at the time, not the big companies they are now. And she was like, "Yeah, they're trying to sell into Fortune 500 companies. One of them is actually trying to land a Fortune 10 right now. And they said the thing that's holding them back is they don't have compliance certification, they don't have a SOC 2. (00:25:08): "And I told them, 'Hey, what if I do that for you?' And they were like, 'Oh, you can just do that?'" And she was like, "Yeah." And she did it, and they landed the deal. And it's one of the clearest examples to me of a product that satisfies a promise, but this product is going to unlock revenue for you. You are going to be able to land this enterprise deal. And so I think they just did a phenomenal job of that. And that's what you're looking for when you're at level one, a problem that really matters to three to five customers.
turns.zh: B2B版的Alexa。当时她还有个想法，关于代发货（dropshipping）的，但她对代发货一无所知。她一直处于那种模式——“我们先开发产品，再看看有没有人需要”。后来她意识到这种方法行不通，于是改变策略。她开始与潜在客户交流，特别关注安全问题，以及为什么很多初创公司不使用安全产品。（00:23:48）：她与安全工程师、首席信息安全官、首席技术官和初创公司负责人交谈，问他们：“在安全方面，你们最痛恨的工作是什么？” 对方反复回答：“填写安全问卷、进行合规审计，这些都是繁琐的手动工作。我们要填写表格、截取AWS账户的屏幕截图，整个流程毫无意义。” 她自己在使用Dropbox Paper时也深有体会，当时获取SOC 2认证的过程非常繁琐。（00:24:26）：她之所以需要获取SOC 2认证，是因为我们想将Dropbox Paper推向企业市场。于是她对我说：“市场上有这样的痛点，我觉得我能解决它，或许还能带来营收增长。” 我问：“你怎么说？” 她回答：“我找到了首批客户或设计合作伙伴，比如Segment、Front和Figma。” 那时是2017、2018年，这些公司当时规模还小，不是如今的大型企业。她说：“是的，他们正试图向《财富》500强企业销售产品，其中一家甚至正争取拿下《财富》10强客户。但阻碍他们的关键问题是没有合规认证，没有SOC 2认证。” 我说：“那我来帮你们做怎么样？” 他们惊讶地说：“真的吗？” 她回答：“是的。” 她做到了，最终拿下了订单。这对我来说是产品满足承诺的最典型案例——这款产品能为你带来营收增长，让你成功拿下企业订单。我认为他们在这方面做得非常出色。这正是第一阶段所追求的——找到真正为三到五个客户创造价值的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That specific example, I think she delivered a spreadsheet. There was no product, she just manually filled out a spreadsheet and gave it to them.
turns.zh: 那个具体例子，我记得她提供的是一份电子表格。当时没有产品，她只是手动填写表格然后交给客户。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Completely manual. She was the one behind the email address posing as the AI, but doing it herself. And I think that's revealing of it's okay to be inefficient at level one, as long as you are delivering incredible satisfaction.
turns.zh: 完全手动操作。她用AI账号发邮件，但实际都是她自己在操作。我觉得这充分说明了第一阶段可以不追求效率，只要能提供超高满意度就行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was just going to say that. This is the ultimate example of efficiency is not important, which I love, is what you're pointing out at this step. I know you're going to share another example, but just to summarize what this stage feels like from earlier when you talked about, essentially, of less than 10 people, you're trying to find three to five customers. I think that's so important. You're not trying to find tens or hundreds, you're just like, "Three to five people." And the customer element, I imagine, you're implying they're paying you money.
turns.zh: 是啊，我正想说这点。这个例子完美诠释了效率不重要的重要性，我太爱这个观点了。你刚刚提到这个阶段的关键点——少于10人的团队，目标是找到三到五个客户。我觉得这太重要了。你不是去找几十个、几百个客户，而是专注于“三到五个人”。而且客户层面，我猜你指的是他们愿意付钱给你们吧？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yes, they're paying you money and you're delivering a product that solves a problem for them.
turns.zh: 是的，他们付钱给你，而你提供的产品能为他们解决一个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the product could be potentially a spreadsheet or super Wizard of Oz at this point even.
turns.zh: 而且这个产品现在甚至可能只是一份电子表格，或者一个超级《绿野仙踪》式的项目。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah, that's okay at this level.
turns.zh: 嗯，在这个阶段这没关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know RAMP actually had barely a product when they started selling. Initially, they had someone just updating things behind the scenes on these dashboards. And then you talked about the problem needs to be important and urgent, which connects to people paying attention to a startup that they don't trust or know anything about because the problem is that important and urgent. And you also mentioned it has to satisfy a promise you're giving them, "We'll solve SOC 2 for you," and then you actually accomplish that.
turns.zh: 我知道RAMP刚开始销售时几乎没有产品。最初，他们只是在后台更新这些仪表板上的数据。然后你提到问题必须重要且紧迫，这与人们关注一家他们不信任或不了解的初创公司有关，因为问题足够重要和紧迫。还有你提到必须兑现给他们的承诺，比如"我们会为你解决SOC 2合规问题"，然后你确实做到了。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else maybe as a benchmark that tells you you're at this step of product-market fit?
turns.zh: 有没有其他基准可以表明你达到了产品-市场匹配的这个阶段？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So like I said, you're pre-seed less than 10 people. Probably, your demand source at this stage is mostly people you know. It's friends and family, it's your network, maybe it's VCs. You haven't probably done a lot of cold outreach at this point, and it's hard to find customers. You're trying to get three to five. It probably takes you 20 warm intros to get one, something along those lines. So maybe to get to three to five, it's at least 50 conversations. That's very normal at this stage because you're just trying to find the right problem and find customers who have it. You're probably in the $0 to 500K ARR, somewhere in that zone. I would say that you're at level one. (00:27:48): And then there are metrics to track efficiency, things like burn multiple, gross margin, NRR all of these things. All of them are just not applicable at this stage. It's too early and you shouldn't be worrying about that stuff. And so you want to be feeling this sense of progress that there are customers who need what you are building and the thing you're building works. And so conversely, the signs that we see a lot of founders get stuck, and this is a very common level to get stuck. And so if you're hanging out here for six months, nine months, 12 months, and there's yellow flags that are appearing, you're starting to feel stuck. (00:28:24): And so the yellow flags are something like, let's say, your product disappeared overnight, your customers wouldn't be super disappointed. Let's say you have a handful of happy customers. Let's say you've got four or five customers, but the most important feature is actually different for each one of them. That starts to look a little bit more like a consulting business than a product business. Or it just feels incredibly hard to find the marginal customer, the next new customer. Or your usage is low. The product is in their hands, but the usage is low, it's not growing that much. It lasts for six months. (00:28:55): And I think, there's a really good example, Jack Altman, who's the founder of Lattice, he founded Lattice in 2015. We've talked to him a bunch on the First Round Paths to Product-Market Fit and other things. So for those who don't know, Lattice is a people management platform, but it didn't start that way. And most people don't know about this, Lattice actually started as an OKR tool back in 2015.
turns.zh: 有的。就像我说的，你处于种子前阶段，员工不到10人。这个阶段你的需求来源主要是熟人。可能是朋友、家人、社交圈，甚至是风投公司。此时你可能还没有做太多冷电话推销，客户很难找到。你正努力争取3-5个客户。可能需要20次暖场沟通才能获得一个客户，类似这样。所以要达到3-5个客户，至少需要50次沟通。这在现阶段很正常，因为你只是在寻找正确的问题，寻找有需求的客户。你可能处于0到50万美元的年度经常性收入区间，大概在这个范围内。我认为你处于第一阶段。（00:27:48）：然后有一些衡量效率的指标，比如烧钱倍数、毛利率、净客户保留率等，但这些在现阶段都不适用。太早了，不该操心这些。关键是要感受到进展感——有客户需要你正在开发的产品，而且产品能正常运行。相反，我们看到很多创始人卡在这一阶段的迹象，这是一个常见的卡点阶段。如果你在这一阶段停留6个月、9个月、12个月，却出现黄旗警告，你就开始感觉卡住了。（00:28:24）：黄旗警告可能包括，比如产品一夜之间消失，客户不会特别失望。假设你有几个满意的客户，但每个客户最重要的功能却各不相同。这开始更像是一家咨询公司，而不是产品公司。或者很难找到边际客户，新的新客户。或者产品使用率低，产品在他们手中，但使用率不高，增长不明显。这种情况会持续6个月。（00:28:55）：我觉得有个很好的例子，Lattice的创始人杰克·奥特曼。他在2015年创立了Lattice。我们在First Round的Product-Market Fit之路等节目中多次采访过他。大家可能不熟悉，Lattice最初是一款OKR工具，但2015年并非如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, didn't know.
turns.zh: 哦，我不知道啊。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. And so Jack had just seen this at other companies. He's like, "Okay, companies are doing OKRs, but they're not very good at it and it causes a lot of arguments among the executive team and employees are noncompliant. They think the whole thing's dumb. So I can fix that with software." And so the original version of Lattice was for managing OKRs. And he was able to sell it. And so his buyer was the head of HR, and they said, "Okay, yeah, we'll give this a shot." And he had a couple companies using it, and they would use it for one quarter. And then the next quarter would come around, and they were like, "Didn't go that well last time. I don't know, the employees don't seem to like it. I don't know." (00:29:59): And then the quarter after that, they were like, "No, we're not buying this, we're not using this." And so Jack pulled off the pivot to people management. And the way that he did it was he actually kept the persona. And so this gets into the ideas of the four Ps, and I'll talk about this a little bit more. This is our version of the four Ps. You've got the persona, the problem, the promise, and the product. And all four of these things have to line up. Your product has to deliver a promise that solves the problem of your persona. And so Jack actually kept the persona. He was like, "I've gotten to know these heads of HR really well over the last six to nine months. I text with them, I go out to coffee with them, I'm friends with them, I know them really well. This OKR thing just doesn't seem to be a big deal for them, but they've got other problems that I could look at solving." (00:30:53): And the interesting thing was that timing, it was mid-2010s, performance management had started to come back in favor. It was like this pendulum. There was a period of time where performance management was really important, and then all these companies were like, "We're not doing this anymore." And then the pendulum swung back, and around 2015, 2016 was that time. And so Jack literally showed them Figma mock-ups. There was no product, but he's like, "What if I could solve performance management for you in a way that is much more modern and much more employee-friendly and manager-friendly and the whole thing's just going to work better?" (00:31:25): And the response was off the charts. And people wanted this thing. And I believe he sold his first five or 10 customers with Figma mock-ups. Before, he hadn't built anything really. And so that, I think, is an interesting example of he was stuck in the zone of people didn't love what he was doing. He kept the persona, but he changed the problem that he was solving and the promise he was delivering through the product. And we do a whole section on pivots and when to pivot and how to pivot. And I think this is actually the best framework for this, is the four Ps. Lattice kept the first one but changed the others. Vanta changed all four. (00:32:08): There are other products like Plaid that actually kept elements of the product they were doing. So I don't know if you know the story of Plaid, but Zach Perret was building... Plaid started out not as like a API for bank accounts. It started out as a consumer budgeting app. It was a consumer app. And it just was supposed to help you save money and budget and stuff. And it just wasn't that popular. And the founders were frustrated, but they had built this part of the product that enabled the app to connect to your bank accounts, and had solved all the nitty-gritty issues with that. And then they found that their friends wanted to license it from them. (00:32:46): So Zach had a friend at Venmo who wanted to license this, and they got Robinhood at some point, they got Coinbase at some point. So that's an example of they actually kept a lot of the code that they had written. They kept the product, but they completely changed the other three Ps. Instead of solving for consumers who have a problem with budgeting, we are going to solve for developers at fintech companies who have a problem connecting to bank accounts. And it was a total flip of the four Ps. But that's why I really like this framework because I think it really helps founders think in a structured way about this.
turns.zh:
是的。杰克之前在其他公司见过这种情况。他说：“好吧，其他公司都在做OKR，但他们做得很不好，导致高管团队和员工之间经常发生争执，员工们也觉得这整个事情很愚蠢。所以我可以用软件来解决这个问题。” 最初的Lattice版本就是用于OKR管理的。他成功卖出了这款产品，买家是人力资源部主管，他们说：“好吧，我们可以试试看。” 有几家公司用了一个季度，但下一个季度就反馈效果不佳。再下一个季度，他们干脆放弃了。于是杰克转向了人员管理领域。他的策略是保留原有的用户画像。接下来我会详细讲解“四P理论”——用户画像、问题、承诺、产品。这四个要素必须协同一致。产品必须兑现承诺，解决用户痛点。而杰克成功保留了用户画像。他说：“过去六到九个月，我和这些人力资源主管建立了深厚的友谊。我们会互发短信，一起喝咖啡，他们很信任我。我发现OKR对他们来说不是大问题，但他们还有其他我能解决的难题。” 

2010年代中期是一个转折点。绩效管理重新受到重视，犹如钟摆效应。曾有一段时间，绩效管理被视为核心要务，但许多公司后来放弃了。2015年前后，这种趋势又卷土重来。杰克向客户展示了Figma设计原型，虽然产品尚未成型，但他提议：“如果我能用更现代、更人性化的方式解决绩效管理问题，员工和管理者都会受益。” 反响热烈，客户纷纷下单。

成功的关键在于：保留用户画像，调整解决的问题和产品承诺。我们在书中详解了转型的四要素——用户画像、问题、承诺、产品。Lattice保留了第一要素，但调整了其他要素；Vanta则彻底重构了全部四要素。还有Plaid这样的案例——虽然保留了部分原有功能，但最终将其授权给其他公司。
（00:32:46）：所以扎克在Venmo有个朋友想授权这项技术，他们后来收购了Robinhood，还收购了Coinbase。这就是一个例子，他们实际上保留了自己编写的大量代码。他们保留了产品本身，但彻底改变了其他三个P（产品、价格、渠道、促销）。我们不再为有预算问题的人群解决难题，而是为金融科技公司的开发者解决与银行账户对接的难题。这完全颠覆了传统的四P营销理论。但这正是我特别喜欢这个框架的原因，我认为它能真正帮助创业者以结构化的方式思考这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Todd, this is amazing. I'm so happy we're doing this. I think this is going to help a lot of people. I want to move on to level two, but first let me try to summarize some of these key elements. So these four Ps is essentially what you should try to change if you're stuck in this level or any level. And just to summarize, you can change who you're targeting, the persona, you can change the problem you're solving, you could change the way you're pitching it, which is the promise is how you describe it, basically positioning. And then you could also just change your product. You mentioned Vanta changed all four, some companies change just one. Any advice for how to know which of these to change? What points you to change this versus change that? Is there anything that you've seen?
turns.zh: 托德，这太棒了。我很高兴我们能做这件事。我觉得这会对很多人有所帮助。我想进入第二阶段，但首先让我总结一下这些关键要素。也就是说，如果你卡在当前阶段或任何阶段，关键在于改变以下四点：目标客户群（persona）、解决的问题、推销方式（promise，即产品定位）以及产品本身。你提到Vanta把这四点都改了，有些公司只改其中一项。关于如何判断该改哪一项，有什么建议吗？哪些因素会促使你选择某个方向而非其他？你有没有遇到过相关案例？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think different founders approach this differently. And I've seen a lot of founders who are build first and then sell, and I've seen a lot of founders who are sell first and then build. And they can both work. I tend to gravitate towards the, "I want to sell it before I build it," because I really want the signal from customers and I want that to be the guide and the oxygen that drives what I'm building. I find that very motivating. I also find it easier, honestly. (00:34:25): Rather than guessing like, "Oh, I'm going to write 50,000 lines of code and then see if somebody wants this thing," I think it's better to talk to a bunch of customers, know that, "Hey, if I had this thing, if I could build this thing, I know it would sell. I know these people want this thing." So I tend to approach it from that point of view and therefore, I focus on the persona and the problem and the promise. What is the promise that is really going to click for that buyer, for that persona? And then the product's job is to satisfy those first three Ps really.
turns.zh: 我认为不同创始人的方法各不相同。我见过很多创始人先开发再销售，也见过很多先销售再开发的。两种方法都能奏效。我个人倾向于“先卖再做”的模式，因为我非常希望从客户那里获得反馈，让客户的需求成为我开发产品的指引和动力。说实话，我发现这样做更容易。（00:34:25）与其盲目猜测“哦，我先写5万行代码，再看看有没有人买”，不如先和一群客户交流，确认“如果我能开发出这个产品，我知道它一定能卖出去，用户肯定需要它”。所以我会从这个角度出发，重点关注目标客户群、解决的问题和产品定位。什么样的承诺才能真正打动目标客户？而产品的核心任务就是要完美满足前三个要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And obviously, those are much easier to change and play with versus rebuilding your product. So if nothing else, you should probably start there. I actually have a post with a bunch of awesome examples of changing the positioning, changing the persona, and so we'll link to that in show notes if people want more examples. Finally, let me try to summarize the stage. So I think it's important to note at this nascent stage, it's not roaring product-market fit. It's, as you described, very nascent. You're getting customers, but it's hard. You said it's 20 introductions to one sale, but you're getting them. (00:35:25): I know Retool has a great quote. David has this quote of, "Every customer he got early on, he felt it was the last customer he was ever going to get. No more people want this thing and it's always a struggle." So I think that's very normal, is what you're describing. The beginnings are rarely off and to the right. And it's okay if this takes a while. You said that if you spent 12 months at this stage, you're probably stuck in the stage, and signs that you're stuck in this nascent stage versus this is actually normal. Signs you mentioned are if you ask people if this went away and they wouldn't be disappointed, they'd be like, "Nah, all right. It's cool." (00:36:01): You have many customers, but they're using different features of the product. So to you, the way you described it, essentially, you're professional services for them. You're not actually building a product. You consult a lot of people. And then they're actually not using it often. They're buying, they're paying for it, like the last example, but they're not necessarily using it and they're going to churn pretty quickly.
turns.zh: 显然，与重新打造产品相比，调整定位和用户画像要容易得多。所以即便没有别的办法，你或许也应该从这里入手。我实际上有一篇帖子，里面列举了许多改变定位、转换用户画像的绝佳案例，如果大家想获取更多示例，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。最后，让我来总结一下现阶段的情况。在这个初级阶段，产品与市场的契合度显然尚未达到理想状态。正如你所描述的，它还处于萌芽阶段。你正在获取客户，但过程困难重重。你说要20次推广才能达成一次销售，但至少你还在推进。（00:35:25）：我知道Retool有一句很棒的名言。大卫曾说：“早期获得的每个客户，我都觉得那将是最后一个客户。没人再需要这个产品了，一切都举步维艰。” 所以你所描述的这种情况很正常。初期阶段很少一帆风顺。如果这个阶段拖延太久，你很可能陷入停滞状态。判断是否停滞的关键信号包括：当你问客户是否会因为产品消失而失望时，他们不会感到失望，反而会说：“不会啦，挺好的。” （00:36:01）：你有很多客户，但他们使用的产品功能各不相同。用你描述的方式来说，本质上你是在为他们提供专业服务，而不是真正在开发产品。你为很多人提供咨询服务，但用户实际使用频率很低。他们购买了产品，付了钱，就像上一个例子那样，但使用率不高，流失率也会很高。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anything else you wanted to touch on there before we get to level two?
turns.zh: 在进入第二阶段之前，你还有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: The last thing that I'd add at level one is there's this founder from a company called Persona, his name is Rick Song. He's super awesome. Persona is a First Round company. They do identity verification. And Rick's analogy, I just love it for level one, is you don't want to get friend-zoned by your customers, where your customers like you, but they don't love you and they don't need you. And he was super paranoid about this in the early days of Persona. And his technique for doing this, which I really like, is super simple, was he was very close with his first five or 10 customers. (00:37:00): And he would go to them and sit them down one-on-one and say, "I need your help. It is very important to me that this company succeeds and does not fail. So I don't want you to be nice to me. I want you to tell me is Persona a necessity for your company? If we went away, how painful would that be? If a competitor came along that charged half as much as us, would you switch to them?" And he's really trying to get to the essence of: is Persona critical for you or am I in the friend zone? And I just think that's a really great way of thinking about this.
turns.zh: 在第一阶段，我想补充的一点是，来自Persona公司的创始人Rick Song。他非常出色。Persona是First Round投资的公司，专注于身份验证。Rick的比喻让我印象深刻，非常适合第一阶段：你不想被客户“友情区化”。客户可能喜欢你，但不爱你，也不需要你。他在Persona早期就对此深有警惕。他的方法很简单，就是与前五到十位客户建立紧密联系。（00:37:00）：他会单独找他们坐下来问：“我需要你们的帮助。对我来说，公司成功至关重要，不能失败。所以别对我客气，请告诉我：Persona对你们是必不可少的吗？如果我们消失了，会有多痛苦？如果有竞争对手收费只有我们的一半，你们会换去他们那儿吗？” 他就是想探寻：Persona对你们至关重要，还是我只是被当作朋友？我觉得这真是思考这个问题的好方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story. It's like in a relationship, it's the talk.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个故事。这就像谈恋爱时的深入沟通。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: It's the talk.
turns.zh: 就是那种深入的交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "Are we a thing?" I love that. That's so good. The sooner you know the truth, the better. And it's hard to hear bad news, but I love that, just advice of just sit them down one-on-one. Let me tell you about CommandBar. If you're like me and most users I've built product for, you probably find those little in-product pop-ups really annoying, "Want to take a tour?" "Check out this new feature." And these pop-ups are becoming less and less effective since most users don't read what they say. They just want to close them as soon as possible. (00:38:08): But every product builder knows that users need help to learn the ins and outs of your product. We use so many products every day and we can't possibly know the ins and outs of everyone. CommandBar is an AI-powered toolkit for product growth, marketing and customer teams to help users get the most out of your product without annoying them. They use AI to get closer to user intent. So they have search and chat products that let users describe what they're trying to do in their own words, and then see personalized results like customer walkthroughs or actions. (00:38:36): And they do pop-ups too, but their nudges are based on in-product behaviors like confusion or intent classification, which makes them much less annoying and much more impactful. This works for web apps, mobile apps and websites, and they work with industry-leading companies like Gusto, Freshworks, HashiCorp and LaunchDarkly. Over 15 million end-users have interacted with CommandBar. To try out CommandBar, you can sign up at commandbar.com/lenny and you can unlock an extra 1,000 AI responses per month for any plan. That's commandbar.com/lenny. Let's talk about level two. So what does level two look like? And what should founders be focusing on when they're in level two?
turns.zh: “我们是不是有戏？”我超爱这句话。这太棒了。越早知道真相越好。但听到坏消息确实难受，不过我喜欢这种做法——就是单独坐下来和用户谈谈。让我跟你讲讲 CommandBar。如果你和我以及我服务过的大多数用户一样，你可能觉得那些产品内弹窗真的很烦人，比如“想参观一下吗？” “看看这个新功能”。但这些弹窗的效果越来越差，因为大多数用户根本不看内容，只想尽快关掉它们。（00:38:08）不过每个产品开发者都知道，用户需要帮助才能深入了解你的产品。我们每天用那么多产品，根本不可能掌握每个产品的所有细节。CommandBar是一款为产品增长、营销和客户团队打造的AI驱动工具包，能帮助用户充分利用你的产品，同时不让他们感到厌烦。它利用AI技术深入理解用户需求。用户可以通过搜索和聊天功能，用自己的语言描述操作需求，随即就能看到个性化结果，比如客户操作指南或操作步骤。（00:38:36）他们也会用弹窗，但这些提示是基于用户在产品内的行为数据，比如用户遇到困惑或行为分类结果，这样既减少了烦感，又提升了效果。它适用于网页应用、移动应用和网站，已与Gusto、Freshworks、HashiCorp和LaunchDarkly等行业领先公司合作。超过1500万终端用户使用过 CommandBar。想试用 CommandBar，可以访问commandbar.com/lenny注册，任意套餐每月可额外解锁1000条AI回复。就是commandbar.com/lenny。接下来聊聊第二阶段。那么第二阶段是什么样的？处于第二阶段的创始人应该重点关注什么？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So level two is developing product-market fit, and your job at level two is now you've got to go from five satisfied customers to 25 satisfied customers. And so now you've got to start thinking about demand in addition to satisfaction. Because it is very hard to just grind your way all the way to 25 customers with sheer willpower, but you can do that to five, maybe 10. And we see some founders who just have phenomenal willpower and grit and grind their way to five or 10 customers. To get to 25 and to get beyond 25, the product has to be doing a lot of the heavy lifting for you. And so that is the essence of this level. (00:39:58): So if you're at this level, now you're seed or Series A style company, maybe you've got up to 20 people at the company. And you're starting to work on this demand source where you have the early signs of a scalable channel, and it's not just warm intros from your VCs or from your friends. You're maybe investing in cold outreach and getting that tuned and humming. You might be investing in content, you might be doing community events, but the whole idea is you're trying to scale the demand source. It's still not easy. A benchmark, we would say, is that your sales conversion without a warm intro is still probably 10%, something like that. (00:40:38): First call to close one is around 10%. If you get higher than that, that's great, but that sort of benchmark for this level. You're in anywhere from the 500K to five million ARR zone, that's a hallmark of level two. And you're actually starting to think about efficiency metrics and sales metrics. You might starting to be thinking about magic number, which is a new ARR that you take in in a period divided by the CAC you spend in that period, so something in the 0.5 to 0.75 range. You want to get higher eventually, but that's pretty reasonable for this level. (00:41:10): You're just starting to think about retention. You've been around for a year, so you've got renewals and you want those renewals renewing. Maybe something like 10%, 20% regretted churn is okay. You don't want to be higher than that, and you want your NRR to be at least 100%. And then things like gross margin and burn multiple, they're still not the focus. Those are the classic efficiency metrics. They're not the focus right now. (00:41:30): But we would say you want your gross margin to be not worse than 50%, and you'd want your burn multiple to be not worse than five X. Your burn multiple, by the way, is just how much you burn in a current period versus how much new ARR comes in. So if you burn $5 million and you take in one, then you've got to burn multiple of five. And you don't want to be worse than that at this stage.
turns.zh:
是的。第二阶段是开发产品与市场的契合度，你在这一阶段的任务是从五个满意的客户扩展到25个客户。因此，你现在需要开始考虑需求问题，而不仅仅是客户满意度。因为仅凭意志力很难一步步发展到25个客户，但五个或十个客户还是可以做到的。我们见过一些创始人，他们凭借非凡的意志力和韧性，成功吸引了五到十个客户。但要达到25个客户甚至更高的目标，产品本身必须为你分担大部分工作。这就是这个阶段的核心。

（00:39:58）：如果你处于这个阶段，现在你可能是一家种子期或A轮融资阶段的公司，公司规模可能已达20人。你开始着手开发需求来源，此时你已初步建立可扩展的渠道，这不再只是风投或朋友的口口相传。你可能开始投入冷邮营销，优化其效果，或着手内容营销、社区活动等，但核心目标是扩大需求来源。尽管这依然不易，但我们认为无需预热的销售转化率仍应保持在10%左右。

（00:40:38）：首次成交的平均时间约为10%。若能提升至此水平固然理想，但这只是该阶段的基准。你的年经常性收入（ARR）应在50万至500万美元之间，这是第二阶段的标志。此时你开始关注效率指标和销售数据，或许会计算“魔术数字”（新ARR除以当期客户获取成本CAC），理想范围为0.5至0.75之间。虽然短期内难以达成更高目标，但这一标准在当前阶段已相当合理。

（00:41:10）：你开始关注客户留存率。运营一年后，你已有续费客户，需确保续费率稳定。10%至20%的客户流失率尚可接受，但NRR（净推荐值）应至少达100%。毛利率和现金流倍数目前仍非核心关注点，这些是经典的效率指标。

（00:41:30）：但毛利率不应低于50%，现金流倍数不应超过5倍。现金流倍数指当前周期烧钱与新ARR的比例。例如，若本周期烧钱500万美元，新ARR仅1美元，现金流倍数即为5倍。当前阶段不宜更差。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. There's a lot of these benchmarks which I love. I imagine not everyone's going to hit each of them exactly. These are just rough guidelines of like, "You're probably in this stage if you're in this level," right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。有很多这些基准，我很喜欢。我想并非每个人都能完全达到这些标准。这些只是大致的指导方针，比如，“如果你处于这个阶段，那你很可能处于这个级别”对吧？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. There's some wide bars around these metrics. It's just representative of, generally, the stage of five to 25 customers.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。这些指标有很大的灵活性范围。这只是大致代表了五到25个客户的阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. And it's so interesting that people think of product-market fit, as you said, as this binary, "I have it or I don't." And the way you're talking about this is in this level to developing product-market fit, a company has 25 satisfied customers, they're over five million in ARR, a lot of cases they have 20 employees.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。有趣的是，人们把产品与市场的契合度看作是非此即彼的二元选择，正如你所说。而你所讲的这个阶段，在开发产品与市场契合度时，公司已有25个满意的客户，ARR超过500万美元，许多情况下有20名员工。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Between 500K and five million. Yeah.
turns.zh: 介于50万到500万之间。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 500K and five million. They have 20 employees. In theory, you would think this is a roaring success. They're killing it, they have all these customers, they're growing. But it's still just level two of product-market fit. So I think this has a really interesting insight, and it reminds me of when I did a bunch of research on product-market fit. (00:42:49): So many founders are like, "I never felt that product-market fit. I didn't have it. It was always, 'I don't know, maybe when we get to 100 million ARR, I'll really feel like we got this.'" So I think this is a really good reminder that a lot of times you're not actually going to feel so confident this will last, and you're going to get to lasting durable product-market fit. So I think that's a really great insight here.
turns.zh: 50万到500万。他们有20名员工。理论上，你可能会认为这是一个巨大的成功。他们做得很好，拥有大量客户，业务在不断增长。但这仍然只是产品-市场匹配的第二阶段。所以我认为这是一个非常有趣的见解，让我想起我曾对产品-市场匹配进行大量研究的经历。（00:42:49）许多创始人会说：“我从未感受到产品-市场匹配。我没有做到这一点。总是觉得‘等我们达到1亿美元的年度经常性收入（ARR）时，我才会真正觉得我们成功了。’” 所以我认为这是一个很好的提醒，提醒我们很多时候并不会真正对业务的持续性充满信心，也不会真正获得持久的产品-市场匹配。所以我认为这里有一个非常好的洞察。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. And the thing that's really, I think, the hallmark of level two is you've got a product that a handful of people like. It's satisfying a critical need for them. Now you've got to open the demand floodgates so that we can get to 25 customers and beyond. And different companies do this in very different ways. It's much easier said than done. Looker is an example. So Looker is a First Round company founded in 2012 by Lloyd Tabb. They do business intelligence. And Looker is interesting because they spent actually a long time at level one, but then flew through level two. And the reason is because Lloyd, the founder, the first five customers of Looker, he was basically going in and doing consulting for them. (00:43:59): And the reason is because of the nature of the product. People don't get Looker until they see their own data in it, and their data is modeled and they see the dashboards and they're like, "Oh, my God. Wow, I didn't realize these insights." So Lloyd understood Looker is not a product you could sell with Figma mock-ups. And so what happened was Lloyd would go into these customers, spend 20, 30, 40 hours before they were even a customer, modeling their data, teaching them how to use it, showing more people within the organization the power of the data and the dashboards. (00:44:32): And later, they called this their forward deploy process. This is how they figured out sales. And so it actually took them a long time in level one to get this right, but then they were able to do this repeatably. And so they went from five to 25 fairly quickly, and a lot of amazing... 75% close rate because they were only selling customers who were already using it. There was zero churn. And Lloyd explains once he got to 20 customers, he's like, "I know I'm onto something. And I think I figured out a model." (00:45:03): And the model stayed the same until they ended up selling to Google. And so they did these other things too. They started focusing on demand channels. They got a couple SDRs who were prospecting. I think they did some partner marketing with AWS Redshift. They did these look-and-tell customer events in San Francisco where they got Looker customers together to talk about what they were doing in Looker and how they built the product. But really, the groundwork was set at level one and then they moved really quickly through level two.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为第二阶段的标志是，你有一个少数人喜欢的产品。它满足了他们的关键需求。现在你必须打开需求闸门，这样我们才能达到25个客户及更多。不同的公司有非常不同的做法。这说起来容易做起来难。Looker就是一个例子。Looker是First Round投资的公司，由Lloyd Tabb于2012年创立。他们做商业智能。Looker很有趣，因为他们在第一阶段花了很长时间，但随后迅速通过了第二阶段。原因在于创始人Lloyd最初为Looker的头五个客户提供咨询服务。（00:43:59）这是因为产品的性质。人们只有在Looker中看到自己的数据、数据被建模、看到仪表板并感叹“天哪，我都没意识到这些洞察”时，才会真正理解Looker。这让Lloyd明白Looker不是一个可以用Figma模型推销的产品。因此，Lloyd会深入这些客户，在他们成为客户前花费20、30、40个小时建模数据，教他们如何使用，向组织内更多人展示数据和仪表板的力量。（00:44:32）后来他们称之为前期部署流程。这就是他们找到销售方法的过程。事实上，他们在第一阶段花了很长时间才做对，但随后能够重复这一过程。他们很快从5个客户增长到25个，转化率高达75%，因为他们只销售已经在使用该产品的客户，没有客户流失。Lloyd解释说，在达到20个客户后，他就意识到：“我知道我找到了正确的方向，我想我找到了一个模式。” （00:45:03）这个模式一直保持到他们最终将业务出售给Google为止。他们还做了其他事情。他们开始关注需求渠道。他们招募了几位销售开发代表进行潜在客户开发。他们与AWS Redshift合作进行伙伴营销。他们在旧金山举办了客户分享活动，邀请Looker客户一起讨论他们在Looker中的应用和产品构建过程。但真正的基础是在第一阶段奠定的，然后他们迅速通过了第二阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So again, the way to think about this phase, is this is when you're starting to scale a way to drive demand. You're not just grinding sales, cold outreach. There's a way you're starting to bring in customers that are more efficient. And in Looker's case, they just started coming because I imagine there's word of mouth and people started to talk about it.
turns.zh: 再次强调，理解这个阶段的关键在于，此时你正着手扩大规模以推动需求增长。不再只是埋头苦干销售、进行冷电话营销，而是开始引入更高效的获客方式。以Looker为例，用户们之所以主动找上门，背后很可能源于口碑传播，人们开始对该产品赞不绝口。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. Let me do another example. A really different example is a company called Ironclad. Ironclad, it's legal. It's a legal tech company founded in 2015. Jason Jason Boehmig is the founder. AI-powered contract management software. So this was interesting because Jason, he started out calling this an AI legal assistant. And in 2024, people are like, "Oh, AI legal assistant. Yeah, that's awesome." But in 2014, people were like, "What?" And he found it really hard to sell. No one was looking for an AI legal assistant. And so he told us this story. (00:46:29): There was an email address on the Ironclad homepage, hello@ironclad.com. This is in 2015. And he doesn't get very much email, but Jason is checking the email. And one day he gets this one line email, and he almost archives it because he doesn't know who it's from and it's one line. But he sees that it's from a person at a publicly-traded company, and so he's like, "Oh, maybe there's something here." And the one line email is just, "Are you a CLM?" And he was like, "What is a CLM?" And he Googles for it. A CLM is a contract lifecycle management platform. And he's reading up about CLMs, and he's like, "Oh, we do that. Yeah." (00:47:08): And so he replies to the email, "Yes, we are a CLM." And the customer gets them on the phone. And the customer says, "Oh, I'm in the market for a CLM. I'm looking at 10 or 12 different vendors, but you guys look pretty cool because there's some automation and some AI stuff going on. Can I check this out?" And Jason's like, "Of course." So he and his co-founder take the train from San Francisco down to San Jose. And on the train, Jason is telling his co-founder, Cai, "Hey, I need you to code this up right now to make it look like what this customer is expecting." (00:47:42): And they get to the meeting, and they do the demo. And the customer has no idea that they just made this demo on the train, and they're a very small company. And they win the contract against these 10 or 12 other established bases, because Ironclad, it's more modern, it's automated, it's got this AI stuff. It's just a better product, or the demo looks like it's going to be a better product. And so Jason reflects on this and he's like, "Yeah, the thing for us is we had been trying to create this new category of AI legal assistant, and it was just a slog. (00:48:10): "And instead, when we changed our positioning to play in an existing category of CLM, but a much better CLM, but customers are already looking for a CLM, they're already looking to spend money on a CLM, and just expand the definition of what that category is, things just started to click." And that's how they got through that zone of 10, 20, 30 customers. And even if you look at the Ironclad website today, it says AI-Powered Contract Management Software. That really is the key idea still.
turns.zh:
是的。让我再举个例子。一个非常不同的例子是一家叫Ironclad的公司。Ironclad是一家合法科技公司，成立于2015年。创始人是杰森·博伊米格（Jason Boehmig）。他们开发的是AI驱动的合同管理软件。这很有趣，因为杰森最初把这项技术称为"AI法律助手"。到了2024年，人们会说："哦，AI法律助手？太棒了。"但在2014年，人们却会说："什么？"他发现很难推销自己的产品，因为当时没人需要AI法律助手。所以他给我们讲了这个故事。（00:46:29）：2015年Ironclad的主页上有一个邮箱地址，hello@ironclad.com。他收到的邮件不多，但他还是会查看。有一天，他收到一封只有一行字的邮件，差点就把它归档了，因为不知道是谁发来的，内容也很简短。但他发现对方是上市公司的人员，于是他想："哦，也许这里面有门道。"那封邮件问："你们是合同生命周期管理平台（CLM）吗？"他回答："什么是CLM？"然后去谷歌搜索。CLM是合同生命周期管理平台。他了解了CLM的相关知识，发现Ironclad正好提供这类服务，于是回复："是的，我们就是CLM。" 对方随即邀请他们去见面。

（00:47:08）：客户问："我们正在寻找CLM产品，看了10到12家供应商，你们看起来很酷，因为有自动化和AI功能，能演示一下吗？"杰森答应后，和联合创始人乘火车从旧金山到圣何塞。在火车上，他对联合创始人蔡（Cai）说："现在就去写代码，让界面符合客户预期。"

（00:47:42）：他们到了会议现场，进行演示。客户完全不知道他们是在火车上临时搭建的演示系统，而且Ironclad是一家小公司。最终他们击败了10到12家老牌供应商，凭借更现代化、自动化的CLM产品赢得了合同。杰森反思道："我们之前试图打造AI法律助手这个新品类，但困难重重。而当我们转向现有品类CLM时，却发现客户已经在寻找CLM解决方案，愿意为此买单。只要扩展CLM的定义范围，一切就顺理成章了。"这就是他们突破前期客户瓶颈的秘诀。即使现在看Ironclad的官网，标语仍是"AI驱动的合同管理软件"，这核心理念至今未变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So this is an awesome example of positioning/promise is the lever they pull here. I love the point about category design. That's one of the ongoing debates on this podcast, whether you should try to create a category.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这是一个绝佳的定位/承诺案例，关键在于他们转换了定位。关于品类设计的观点很值得探讨，也是本播客长期讨论的话题——是该尝试创造新品类，还是顺应已有品类？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I know, it's a hot topic.
turns.zh: 我知道，这是一个热门话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hot topic. Sounds like you're in the boat of probably better not to create your own category.
turns.zh: 热门话题。听起来你可能觉得最好还是别去创造自己的品类。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think it's hard to create a category. It certainly works in some cases, but if you actually have a really interesting spin on an existing category, there's already buyers spending money on that thing. They're already looking for something to buy. So if you can do it, I do actually think that way is easier.
turns.zh: 我觉得创建品类挺难的。当然有些情况下是可行的，但如果你对现有品类有非常有趣的创新思路，那些已经有消费者愿意为此买单的人群，他们本来就一直在寻找要购买的东西。所以如果你能做到这一点，我确实认为这条路更容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get to level three, what are signs that you're maybe stuck at level two, and what should one do about that?
turns.zh: 在我们谈到第三级之前，有哪些迹象表明你可能停留在第二级，以及该如何应对呢？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So the whole idea of level two is this thing that the marginal customer is getting easier. And so you've got to be focusing on demand and the repeatability of demand while you maintain satisfaction. So the yellow flags are things that are the opposite of that. Your current customers are pretty happy, but you're just having trouble opening the floodgates. As you're getting to the top end of level two, you should start to hear some startups know who you are like, "Oh, you need a SOC 2, you're a startup. Oh, Vanta." "Oh, you need AI-powered contract management software. Oh, Ironclad." You start to get known for a thing. (00:49:59): And so if you're having trouble opening those floodgates, and you're sitting there for, I don't know, 12 months, 18 months, that's a problem. Or you have things like your regretted churn is greater than 20%. That's a satisfaction warning sign. And again, you have to maintain the satisfaction as you work on these other things. Every level just gets more things you have to do. Or you could be finding that the sales cycle's taking too long, you're losing deals late in the funnel, you're losing the competitors. You're just not feeling the urgency from customers or you're struggling to hit the price point that you want. (00:50:33): And the way that customers will say this to you because customers are nice, right? They'll say, "Oh, we don't have the budget." Or, "Oh, it's just not the right time for us. We'd love to talk again next year." That means no, when you're hearing that from customers. You want customers who are like, "Oh, of course. Yeah, this is expensive, but I'm going to make this work because I need this." And so if you're seeing any of those signs, those are the signs that you maybe are stuck or plateauing at this level. And I really think it's important to think about the four Ps and think about: how am I going to pivot my way out of this? Jack Altman, who I mentioned earlier from Lattice, he's got a great quote on this. (00:51:14): It's up in a video on the website. What did he say? He said, "Most founders do a 10% pivot, and what they need to be doing is a 200% pivot." Jack didn't say this, but I think part of my interpretation of this is it's psychologically hard as a founder. You've gotten to this many customers, you're starting to plateau, but you're like, "I don't want to throw this whole thing away." But you have to be willing to let go and really focus on nailing the four Ps at this point.
turns.zh: 是的。第二级的核心在于边际客户获取变得更容易了。所以你必须关注需求和需求的可重复性，同时保持客户满意度。而与此相反的黄旗信号则需要警惕。比如现有客户对你挺满意，但你却难以打开增长之门。当你即将突破第二级时，你会开始听到一些创业公司知道你是谁，比如“哦，你需要SOC 2认证，你是创业公司。哦，Vanta。”“哦，你需要AI驱动的合同管理软件。哦，Ironclad。”你开始因某个特定领域而闻名。（00:49:59）：但如果你在打开增长之门时遇到困难，比如已经拖延了12个月、18个月，这就是个问题。或者客户流失率超过20%，这也是满意度警示信号。当然，在处理这些问题时，你必须保持客户满意度。每个级别需要处理的事情都越来越多。或者你可能会发现销售周期过长，漏掉了销售漏斗末端的交易，输给了竞争对手。客户没有紧迫感，或者你难以达到理想的定价点。（00:50:33）：客户会委婉地说“我们没有预算。”或者“现在不是合适的时机，明年再聊。”这意味着不行。当听到这些反馈时，要警惕。理想的客户会说“当然，虽然贵了点，但我需要这个，所以我会想办法解决。”如果你看到这些迹象，那说明你可能停留在这一级，或者停滞不前。我认为重要的是要思考四个P：如何通过转型摆脱困境。之前提到的Lattice的Jack Altman对此有很好的见解。（00:51:14）：视频在网站上有。他说了什么？他说：“大多数创始人只做10%的转型，而他们需要做200%的转型。”Jack没这么说，但我对此的理解是，创始人从心理上很难接受。当你已经积累了这么多客户，却停滞不前时，你会想“我不想放弃整个局面”。但你必须愿意放手，在这个阶段真正专注于做好四个P。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in your experience, do you find, essentially, pivoting is the answer if you're stuck?
turns.zh: 根据你的经验，如果你陷入困境，转型是否就是解决之道？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think sometimes it's nice when it's the Ironclad thing, right?
turns.zh: 有时候像Ironclad这样的例子很棒，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: It's nicest when it's the Looker thing of you don't have to change anything. It just starts working and basically, the whole thing works the whole time. That's not common. It's nice when it's the Ironclad thing when you just change one of them, or maybe two of them. Starting over with all four of these is hard at level two, but oftentimes, it's what's required. I was mentioning earlier, level two is the second most common level to get stuck. (00:52:20): A big chunk of companies are going to get stuck at level one, and the second biggest is at level two. So sometimes it's hard. I think the trap is not doing enough to realize that you're actually not progressing to product-market fit in the way that you need to and just starting to burn money and not make progress. And you've seen many startups struggle with this. I think it's the hardest part of it.
turns.zh: 情况最理想的是，当你遇到“Looker式”的问题时，无需做任何改动。它能迅速上线，基本能一直正常运作。但这种情况并不常见。遇到“Ironclad式”的问题时，只需调整其中一项或两项即可。然而在第二阶段，重新调整全部四项会非常困难。我之前提到过，第二阶段是用户最常卡住的阶段。（00:52:20）许多公司会卡在第一阶段，而第二阶段是第二大卡点。所以有时确实很困难。我认为关键在于，当你意识到自己未能按照预期推进产品-市场匹配时，却仍在烧钱却毫无进展时，这才是最难的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Especially once they're a million, two million, three million ARR and they're like, "Look, we're making all this money." And they don't necessarily realize that they've been stuck at this stage for so long. So just to summarize flags that something is wrong and that you should probably think about changing your persona, your problem, your promise or your product, is it's been 12 to 18 months at this stage of product-market fit. You are churning about 20% of customers. And these are logo churn, I imagine, just like businesses stop using you.
turns.zh: 是的。尤其是当他们的年度经常性收入达到100万、200万、300万美元时，他们会说：“看，我们赚了这么多钱。”但他们往往没有意识到，自己在产品-市场匹配阶段已经卡了很久。所以要总结出一些警示信号，表明可能需要调整用户画像、问题、承诺或产品，那就是在产品-市场匹配阶段停留了12到18个月，客户流失率约20%，而且这些应该是标志性的客户流失，比如企业不再使用你的产品。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your sales cycles are really slow. Is there a sense of what slow means? Just a rough heuristic. What should it...
turns.zh: 你的销售周期非常缓慢。能大概理解“缓慢”是什么意思吗？只是一个粗略的启发。应该怎么做呢？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Well, some sales cycles are slow. If you're selling to companies that are big, you're selling to government, that type of thing. I don't know. Rough rule of thumb is... There's different ACVs also. If you're the kind of product that is 20K, 30K annual contracts, that was Looker, right? But they were able to do the sales cycle very repeatedly because they closed so often. There are some contracts that are 100K, 200K, six figure contracts. Those can take a long time. Those can take three to six months. You can't basically be in the worst of both worlds where you've got a slow sales cycle and a low ACV. That is the quadrant of death basically.
turns.zh: 嗯，有些销售周期确实很慢。比如面向大型企业或政府部门销售，这种情况下周期较长。我不知道。大致的经验法则是……ACV（年度合同价值）也不同。如果你的产品合同金额是2万、3万美元，那就是Looker的情况，对吧？但他们能频繁完成销售，所以销售周期重复得很快。有些合同金额则高达10万、20万美元，甚至六位数的合同。这些可能需要三到六个月才能完成。总之，你不能陷入两难的境地——既有缓慢的销售周期，又低ACV。这基本上就是死亡四象限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. And then the other sign is just you're not finding demand starting to come to you. You're not finding a channel to drive demand. And is a big part of this inbound? You're supposed to start seeing more inbound coming at you? Or is it more just sales becomes easier?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。另一个信号是，你找不到需求主动来找你。你找不到能驱动需求的渠道。入站营销在其中占很大比例吗？你应该开始看到更多主动找上门的需求吗？还是说销售变得更容易了？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: It's both. So sales becomes easier, but I think if you are starting to get to level three, which is where we're getting to next, you've probably got 10%, 20% of your inbound coming or completely organic inbound.
turns.zh: 两者都有。所以销售变得更容易，但我认为当你进入第三阶段（我们接下来要讲的阶段）时，你可能会有10%、20%的入站流量完全是自然产生的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So again, if you're stuck at this stage, and these are signs that are like, "Oh, man, this sounds familiar," your advice is find one of these things to shift the person you're going after, the problem you're solving, the way you position it and/or your product if you have to.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。所以再次强调，如果你卡在这一阶段，这些都是类似“天啊，这听起来太熟悉了”的警示信号。你的建议是，找到其中一项来调整目标客户、解决的问题、定位方式和/或产品（如果有必要的话）。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. And probably just look for something that is a lot more of a burning pain. It's usually that the problem is not significant enough, important enough to people, or the promise is not valuable enough. It's usually one of those [inaudible 00:54:54] assuming you have a reasonable persona.
turns.zh: 是啊。而且可能你只需要找一个更让人感到迫切需要的东西。通常来说，问题要么不够严重，要么对人们来说不够重要，或者承诺的价值不够高。假设你的目标用户群体是合理的，那很可能就是这其中之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And the reason I am spending so much time here, as you said, most companies get stuck here, like B2B SaaS companies. So I think it's really important to make sure people have something to go with. And in the course and in the post you put out, there's more examples of companies going through this and what they did. Let's talk about level three. What does level three look like? What should you be focusing on there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。正如你所说，我之所以在这里花这么多时间，是因为大多数公司都会卡在这一步，比如B2B SaaS公司。所以我觉得确保用户有能产生共鸣的东西非常重要。在你发布的课程和帖子中，还有更多公司经历类似困境并成功应对的案例。接下来聊聊第三级。第三级会是什么样子？你应该重点关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So level three is strong product-market fit. This is where I think it starts to get fun. This is where all the product-market fit adages come in, "The fish are jumping into the boat. The rock is rolling down the hill and I'm trying to chase it instead of pushing it up the hill." And keep in mind, for most enterprise founders, we're now three, four or five years into the company, so it's not easy to get here. And to get to L3 here, you are looking for repeatability. The marginal customer has become much easier. (00:55:48): And so you mentioned, Lenny, this quote from David Hsu from Retool, which I love too, and I'll read it again. He said, "We talked to someone who said that finding product-market fit was so visceral, you immediately felt it like a geyser." And we honestly never felt that in the first couple years. At Retool, every customer we got, whether that was number four or number 14, felt like the last customer we were ever going to find. It felt like rolling the stone uphill, and if you stop pushing, it's going to roll back on you and crush you. (00:56:15): And that's how it felt until we had a few million in ARR. That's when the boulder went down the other side and we had to chase it to keep up. And you mentioned earlier, founders were like, "I'm not sure I ever felt product-market fit." This is when you start to feel it. And Jack Altman, again, from Lattice said, "The biggest shift was in the ease of getting leads." I remember thinking, "I don't even know where these leads are coming from, just more and more of them are showing up each month." (00:56:43): But that is a great feeling. That is a great feeling. Filip Kaliszan from Verkada, he's in some of the videos on our website too. His quote, I'll read it, was, "After our first year of sales in 2018, those next two years were crazy. We were barely keeping up with production. We had to scale all the systems. A lot of things had to happen in the span of 12 to 18 months in order to deliver on everything that customers were hoping the solution was going to do for them. And that in itself was a very formative and tricky part of the journey." (00:57:11): So the benchmarks when you are at level three are now you're probably 30 to 100 people inside your company.
