You're probably at Series B-ish territory in terms of venture, maybe late Series A, maybe early Series C, but probably around Series B. You've really cracked a demand channel. You've cracked marketing and sales. You've got at least one channel that is very scalable. And probably 10% or more of your inbound is coming from just referrals and word of mouth and you're getting known, like we talked about. (00:57:45): ACV ranges are very high. Very wide, I should say. I'd say where you want to get to with level three is 100 customers. And so if you're approaching 100 customers and maybe you have 75K average ACV, that would be strong. You're in this wide zone of five million, all the way up to 25 million ARR. That is very level three. And you're actually starting now to think about some of these efficiency metrics. Remember, we've been punting efficiency. We were saying it shouldn't be worse than a certain number, but it's not a focus. Now, it's got to come into focus. (00:58:20): Because the way that we get to level four is we keep ripping on the satisfaction and the demand, and we tune this thing to get very efficient. So we're talking about our gross margin needs to be above 60%, hopefully above 70%. Our burn multiple is now below three. Ideally, we're close to one. Burn multiple in the one to three zone is where we want to be at level three. Regretted churn's less than 10%, NRR is greater than 110%. These are good benchmarks for this level.
turns.zh:
是的。所以第三级是强产品-市场契合度。这时候我觉得事情开始变得有趣起来了。所有关于产品-市场契合度的谚语都适用，比如“鱼儿跳进船里”、“石头滚下山坡，而我却在追着它而不是把它推上山坡”。要记住，对于大多数企业创始人来说，我们现在已经运营了三到五年，要达到这个阶段并不容易。要达到第三级，你需要寻求可重复性。边际客户变得容易获取得多了。（00:55:48）：伦尼，你提到了Retool的大卫·许的这句话，我也很喜欢，我再读一遍。他说：“我们遇到过有人说，找到产品-市场契合度是如此直观，你会立刻感觉到它像一股泉水般涌现。” 而我们在最初的几年里从未有过这种感觉。在Retool，每个新客户，无论是第四个还是第十四个客户，都感觉像是我们能找到的最后一个客户。就像推石头上山，如果你停止推，它就会滚回来，压死你。 （00:56:15）：直到我们的ARR达到几百万美元时，情况才有所转变。巨石终于滚下了另一边，我们不得不追着它跑。你之前提到，创始人会说：“我不确定自己是否真的感受到了产品-市场契合度。” 这时候你才开始真正感受到它。杰克·奥尔特曼再次提到，Lattice的创始人说：“最大的转变在于获取潜在客户的难易程度。” 我记得当时我在想：“我甚至不知道这些潜在客户从哪里来，每个月就越来越多地出现。” （00:56:43）：但这种感觉太棒了。太棒了。Verkada的菲利普·卡利赞也出现在我们网站的视频里。他说：“2018年我们销售第一年后，接下来的两年简直疯狂。我们几乎跟不上生产进度。所有系统都必须扩容。为了满足客户对解决方案的期望，必须在12到18个月内完成一系列任务。这本身就是旅程中一个非常关键且具有挑战性的阶段。” （00:57:11）：第三级阶段的基准现在是公司内部可能有30到100名员工。在风险投资方面，可能处于B轮左右，或者A轮末期、C轮初期，但很可能是B轮左右。你真正开拓了一个需求渠道。你优化了营销和销售。至少有一个渠道是可扩展的。可能10%或更多的潜在客户来自推荐和口碑，你正在变得知名，正如我们之前讨论的。（00:57:45）：ARV范围很高，应该说范围很广。我认为第三级要达到的目标是100个客户。所以如果你接近100个客户，平均ARV可能是7.5万美元，这就很不错了。你处于500万到2500万ARV的广阔区间。这就是典型的第三级阶段。现在你实际上开始考虑一些效率指标了。记住，我们之前一直在拖延效率问题。我们说效率不应该低于某个数字，但这不是重点。现在，它必须成为关注的焦点。 （00:58:20）：因为要达到第四级，我们必须继续提升用户满意度和需求，并调整系统以实现高效运作。所以我们的毛利率需要超过60%，希望能超过70%。现在我们的损耗倍数低于3倍。理想情况下，接近1倍。损耗倍数在1到3倍的区间内，这正是我们想要的。
达到三级水平。遗憾的是，客户流失率低于10%，净推荐值（NRR）超过110%。这些都是该级别表现的良好基准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hearing level three again tells me level two is basically your pivot from: I'm just grinding customers, selling, pitching, constantly trying to find new people, to level three, where it's coming at you and basically, it's the way you always hear about it, as you described. It's rolling downhill. Fish are jumping in the boat. I haven't heard that one before, but I love this. (00:59:11): So essentially, you found a demand channel. You found a way to get people to come to you. A lot of them are just hearing about you from other people, you don't even know where they're coming from. 10% you said are coming from referrals and you're getting to 100 customers. I actually have another quote from David Hsu at Retool, and he actually said even at 100 customers, he still felt like every customer he was getting was the last one.
turns.zh:
再次听到“第三阶段”这个说法，让我意识到第二阶段其实就是从“我只是埋头开发客户、销售产品、不断寻找新客户”转变到第三阶段的关键节点。正如你所描述的，第三阶段就像滚雪球般势不可挡。客户主动找上门来。这句话我之前没听过，但我很喜欢这种比喻。

（00:59:11）：所以本质上，你找到了需求渠道。你找到了让人们主动找上门的办法。很多客户都是通过别人口口相传才找到你的，你甚至都不知道他们从哪里来的。你提到10%的客户来自推荐，而现在已经有100个客户了。我还记得Retool的David Hsu说过，即使达到了100个客户，他也觉得每个新客户都是最后一个。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's like, "I can't believe we got DoorDash. That's incredible. Okay. I think there's no more. That's it."
turns.zh: 他说：“真不敢相信我们拿下了DoorDash。这太不可思议了。好吧，我觉得没别的了。就这样了。”

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: He is a critical person and critical of himself, but a very high expectations person, let's say.
turns.zh: 他是个对自己要求很严格的人，但同时也是个有着极高期望的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Actually, another quote from Ali Ghodsi from Databricks actually said even at 100 million, he wasn't sure they had product-market fit.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过，Databricks的Ali Ghodsi也说过，即使达到了1亿用户，他也不确定是否找到了产品-市场匹配点。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I mean, come on.
turns.zh: 我是说，拜托。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because he's like, "I don't know." I don't know. He felt like, "This is it. Okay, we're done. We're going to cap out here." And I get that.
turns.zh: 因为他会说：“我不知道。”我也不知道。他觉得：“就是这样了。好吧，我们到头了。就到这儿吧。” 我能理解他的感受。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think if you told many, many pre-seed founders that they'd be able to get to 100 million and not know whether they had product-market fit, they'd probably take that.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果你告诉很多种子期创业者，他们能达到1亿用户却不确定是否找到了产品-市场匹配点，他们可能会欣然接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But I think that's maybe an interesting insight. It's often good to be really paranoid and not feel like, "Okay, we're on our way. Let's start pouring in money. Let's do it."
turns.zh: 但我认为这或许是个有趣的洞察。保持高度警惕，避免掉入“我们已经上路了，开始投入资金吧”的陷阱，往往是成功的关键。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I think that's what makes a lot of the best founders the best.
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是许多顶尖创业者之所以成功的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Indeed. Okay, so level three, anything else that would be useful here? Maybe what are signs that you're struggling at level three, you're stuck?
turns.zh: 确实。好的，那么第三阶段，还有什么有用的信息吗？比如说，第三阶段遇到瓶颈、停滞不前的迹象是什么？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So level three problems. And again, it's hard to get to level three, so awesome work for getting here. But the problems that might start to emerge are you've got a leaky bucket, your NRR is below 90%, or your regretted churn's greater than 10%. Maybe growth is just slowing down. You grew three X each of the prior two years, but you're struggling to do a two X this year. At level three, or five years into the company or so, there's probably a lot of competition. If you've gotten here, you've got something that's working, and people are starting to notice and there's going to be competitors. (01:01:01): And they could be the big competitors, they could be the new startups, but you're going to have to figure out how to navigate probably a tougher market than you entered five years ago. And so maybe you found your first scalable channel, but it's getting saturated, you got to find a new channel. These are the level three problems. Or you're growing, but like I said, with efficiency, you're spending too much money to grow. So you feel like, "Okay, yeah, we can grow at three X year over year, two X year over year, but that's going to push our burn multiple above three again." And that's a little bit of a pickle to be in when you have to trade off growth and spend like that.
turns.zh: 是的。所以这是第三级的问题。再说一次，要达到第三级并不容易，所以能走到这一步真是了不起。但可能开始出现的问题包括：漏斗效应严重、NRR低于90%，或者客户流失率超过10%。也许增长速度正在放缓。过去两年你们每年增长3倍，但今年却难以达到2倍的增长。在第三级，或者说公司成立五年左右时，竞争可能已经非常激烈了。如果你能走到这一步，就意味着你的产品或服务已经得到了市场的认可，用户开始注意到你，竞争对手也会随之而来（01:01:01）。他们可能是大型的竞争对手，也可能是新兴的初创公司，但你必须应对一个比五年前更艰难的市场环境。也许你找到了第一个可扩展的渠道，但现在已经趋于饱和，你需要寻找新的增长途径。这些都是第三级的问题。或者你确实在增长，但正如我所说，由于效率问题，增长需要消耗过多资金。你可能会想：“好吧，我们每年增长3倍、2倍，但这会让我们的烧钱倍数再次超过3倍。”当你必须在增长和成本之间权衡时，这确实是个两难的处境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You make it sound like life's great, level three people are coming at us. I think it's important to note never is it easy, never is it like, "Okay, we're good. Let's just ride this wave. Life's going to get so much easier from now on." It's never easy. As you said, there's all these things, you're always still juggling, you still aren't sure it's going to keep going.
turns.zh: 你说得好像一切都很美好似的，第三级的人们正在向我们涌来。但我认为重要的是要认识到，成功绝非易事，从来都不是“好吧，我们现在很棒，顺势而为就行了。从现在开始生活会变得越来越轻松。”这绝非易事。正如你所说，有各种各样的挑战，你永远在平衡各种事务，你永远不确定事情是否会继续发展下去。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: No, I agree. It's like you're spinning plates, and the higher levels you get, there's more plates. You have to keep spinning. And so at level three and getting to level four, we've got to maintain satisfaction and demand. We cannot let them regress in a market that's getting harder, and we have to really start focusing on efficiency. And the companies that can maintain satisfaction and demand and continue to grow and become really efficient, now we're at level four.
turns.zh: 是的，我同意。这就像是在转盘上保持平衡，级别越高，要平衡的事务就越多。你必须不断保持平衡。在第三级和第四级，我们必须维持用户满意度和需求增长。在日益激烈的市场环境中，我们不能让用户满意度和需求出现倒退，我们必须真正开始关注效率。那些能够维持用户满意度和需求增长，同时变得高效的公司，现在就达到了第四级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about level four. What does that look like? What are some problems people run into there?
turns.zh: 让我们谈谈第四级。它是什么样子的？人们在这一级会遇到哪些问题？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So first of all, congrats. If you get to level four, you have a valuable company. You are probably already a unicorn, and you're starting to think about, "Can I become a decacorn?" And so you've reached the highest levels of satisfaction, demand, and efficiency. And so the benchmarks at level four are like, "Okay, now your team is probably bigger than 100 people, you're Series C, Series D or beyond. You've got more than 100 customers and you're starting to figure out, 'How do I get to 200, 300, eventually 1,000 customers?'" You're beyond 25 million in ARR, so 25 million and up, I think in ARR, it qualifies as level four. And your other metrics are looking really good too. Your sales conversion first call to close one is probably better than 15%, your magic number is greater than one, your tax payback is less than 12 months. (01:03:13): All these things are super awesome. And finally, now you've got your gross margin above 80%. Your burn multiple's ideally less than one at this point, you've got less than 10% churn. You've got greater than 120% NRR. And so now the whole thing is like, "Well, how do I keep growing?" This thing's gotten pretty big. And this is generally when we get to 100 million, especially and beyond, the stage that founders are thinking about, "How do I keep growing by expanding TAM, by expanding total addressable market?" And to expand TAM, I can usually take my product and bring it into new markets, or I start to think about multiple products as a way to expand TAM. (01:03:55): And so this is where you see all the truly great companies, the legendary companies are all able to do that. Vanta has begun to do this. They have the Vanta trust management platform, they've got security questionnaires, they've got vendor risk management. So they're starting to do this. You think of Verkada, who I mentioned before. They started with cloud security cameras, now they do alarms, now they do smoke detectors, now they do badge readers. Stripe has classic Stripe, but they've got Stripe Radar, Stripe Atlas. Square has the Square Stand, Cash App, Square Checking, Square Loans. All the companies that are tens of billions of dollars of value have figured out a way to do this. And it's like the never-ending journey that you said before, Lenny. Like, "Congrats, you got to level four." (01:04:40): But there's just this endless thirst for continued growth. And the interesting thing about that is that it requires finding product-market fit over and over again. Just because you got to level four on your main product doesn't mean product-market fit is free on all these new products. And you've been inside Airbnb and I've been inside Dropbox and Twitter. Getting new products to be successful is hard and it requires this mindset of like, "Yeah, we've got a little bit of advantage because people know who we are, and we have a customer set that hopefully we can layer on new products to. But it's not easy." You have to get into this mindset of product-market fit is never easy, and if we want to continue to grow, we got to find it again and again and maintain that mindset.
turns.zh:
首先，恭喜你！如果你能达到第四级，那说明你的公司已经相当有价值了。你很可能已经是一家独角兽企业，并且开始思考：“我能否成为十角兽？”此刻，你已达到满足度、需求和效率的最高水平。第四级的核心指标包括：团队规模可能超过100人，融资阶段达到C轮或更高阶段，客户数量超过100个，并开始探索如何将客户数量提升至200、300甚至1000个。年度经常性收入（ARR）超过2500万美元，销售转化率首次通话成交率高于15%，客户留存率超过1，税务回报期不超过12个月。这些关键指标都非常出色。

最后，毛利率超过80%，烧钱倍数理想情况下小于1，客户流失率低于10%，续费率超过120%。此时，关键挑战在于如何持续增长。面对如此庞大的规模，创始人们通常会思考如何通过拓展总可寻址市场（TAM）来实现增长。例如，Vanta已开始进军多元化领域，推出Vanta信任管理平台、安全问卷调查和供应商风险管理等产品；Verkada从云安全摄像头起步，如今已拓展至警报系统、烟雾探测器和门禁读卡器等领域；Stripe不仅有经典产品，还推出了Stripe Radar和Stripe Atlas；Square则开发了Square Stand、Cash App和Square Checking等产品。所有市值数十亿美元的巨头都找到了实现多元化增长的路径，正如你之前所说的："恭喜你达到第四级！"但持续增长的渴望永无止境，这意味着需要不断寻找产品与市场的最佳契合点。仅因为主产品达到了第四级，并不意味着新产品也能轻松实现市场匹配。我曾在Airbnb、Dropbox和Twitter内部工作过，深知推出成功新产品绝非易事。这需要保持敏捷思维："虽然我们在现有产品上积累了品牌优势，客户群也为新产品提供了潜在基础，但要想持续增长，必须反复验证产品与市场的契合度。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Casey Winters has this great point also that expectations of customers ever increase. And so you have product-market fit today, but there's going to be better products coming out, they're changing, the world changes. And so not only do you have to worry about competitors, there's just expectations continue to rise. So it's a never-ending battle. To give people a little bit of a broader sense here, what percentage of companies do you find make it through each of these stages in your experience, what are rough numbers you may have in your head?
turns.zh: 凯西·温特斯（Casey Winters）还提出了一个重要观点：客户的期望永远在不断提高。如今你或许达到了产品与市场匹配的阶段，但更好的产品即将问世，市场环境在变化，整个世界也在变化。因此，你不仅要应对竞争对手的挑战，客户的期望也会持续攀升。这是一场永无止境的战斗。为了让大家更直观理解，据你的经验，平均有多少比例的公司能成功度过每个阶段？你心里有没有一个大致的数字？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: The majority of companies, so greater than 50%, probably closer to 60 or 70%, are going to get stuck at L1 or L2. And so that leaves, roughly, let's say, 30% make it to L3 or L4 just in our experience looking broadly. And that's our entire goal. Because again, once you get to L3, you've got a real shot, you've got a real shot at building an awesome company. And so if we get that number, help founders get that number above 30%, imagine if that was 50/50 and half the companies that we were working with at seed were able to get to level three strong product-market fit. I think that would be epic. And I think our founders would... There'd be incredible benefits to the ecosystem from that.
turns.zh: 大多数公司（超过50%，可能接近60%或70%）会卡在L1或L2阶段。以我们的广泛经验来看，大约30%的公司能晋升到L3或L4阶段。这正是我们的核心目标。因为一旦达到L3阶段，你就真正有机会打造一家出色的公司。如果能将这一比例提升至30%以上——想象一下，如果能让50%的种子期公司都能成功达成L3级别的产品与市场匹配，那将是极其了不起的。我相信这对我们的创始人以及整个生态系统都将带来巨大益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So essentially, 60% ish of companies don't make it past L2. And I love the way you're framing it of just, "If we can just get a few more companies further, that makes a massive dent both in the world and the lives of founders and people that want to use products." Another question I wanted to talk about briefly is just again, the timelines of each of these levels. Just in your rough experience, how long do each of these levels roughly take so people can get a sense of like, "Oh, it's taken a lot longer. Maybe there's a problem"?
turns.zh: 好的，基本上60%左右的公司无法突破L2阶段。我很欣赏你用这种方式来阐述问题："只要能让更多公司更进一步，就能对整个行业和创始人以及产品用户的生活产生巨大影响。"我想简要谈谈另一个问题，就是每个阶段的时间线。据你的经验，大致每个阶段需要多长时间？这样人们就能判断是否进展过慢，可能存在问题？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So again, this whole thing probably takes four to six years, and so let's just pick five years as the number to get to level four. I think the way this works, ideally, is you probably take 12 to 18 months to do level one, because that is the most important level, honestly, in my mind because that's where you're really choosing the right persona and the right problem to focus on. And I think just that choice is one of the most important choices that founders make. And the interesting thing, my partner, Josh Kopelman, talks about this all the time, is that founders spend 99% of their time building because that's what they've done. (01:07:53): And they spend 1% of their time picking, in picking the market, picking the problem, picking the customer. And in reality, it's that pick that determines the constraints and the boundaries of where you're going to be working for the next, hopefully, 10 years of your life. So there's a real imbalance there. And I actually think that that pick is the most important thing. So I would actually like to spend, let's say, somewhere 12 to 18 months in level one, just really figuring that out and figuring out my four Ps. And then, hopefully, I move very quickly. It takes me a while to get to my first five satisfied customers, but they love it. (01:08:28): And then I go quickly through L2, maybe that takes about a year. This is like the Looker path, the happy path. And then L3 is long just because we're going all the way from five million in revenue up to 25, and that might take a year or two, probably two years even in a good case. And then getting from 25 to 100 million is hard, obviously very hard. And then that probably takes a couple years. And then you're figuring out all of these things. (01:08:53): You're growing your team and your company's got a lot more moving parts and functions, and there's a demand generation side of the house and sales and there's engineering and the whole thing just gets more complicated with a lot more people. But I think that if you set the foundation really nicely at level one and level two that hopefully the whole thing... The boulder is rolling down the hill and it's carrying you forward and you don't just feel like you're pushing this rock uphill for five years. That's not a fun place to be.
turns.zh: 再次强调，这整个过程可能需要四到六年，所以我们就暂定五年作为达到第四阶段的目标。我认为理想的操作流程是，花12到18个月完成第一阶段，因为这确实是最重要的阶段。在我看来，因为在这里你真正要做的是选择正确的目标客户群体和需要解决的问题。而这种选择，往往是创业者做出的最重要的决策之一。我的合伙人乔希·科普尔曼（Josh Kopelman）经常强调，创业者99%的时间都在埋头开发产品，因为这是他们最擅长的。而1%的时间用于选择市场、问题和客户。实际上，这个选择决定了你未来十年职业生涯的边界和限制。所以这里存在着严重的失衡。我认为这个选择是最关键的。所以我希望自己能在第一阶段花12到18个月的时间，真正理清思路，确定我的四个核心要素。然后希望能迅速推进到第二阶段。第一阶段需要花费一些时间才能获得五个满意的客户，但这些客户会非常喜欢你的产品。（01:07:53）：接下来进入第二阶段，大约需要一年的时间。这是典型的Looker路径，快乐阶段。第三阶段则漫长得多，因为我们要从500万营收增长到2500万，可能需要一到两年，甚至在理想情况下也要两年。然后从2500万增长到1亿显然非常困难，恐怕也要花费几年时间。在此期间，你的团队会不断壮大，公司运作的各个环节和职能也将日益复杂，会有市场推广、销售、工程等部门，整个局面会因人员增加而变得更加复杂。但我认为，如果你在第一和第二阶段打下了坚实基础，那么整个过程……就像巨石从山上滚落，推动你前进，而你就不会觉得自己在山上徒劳攀登五年了。那种感觉可不好受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of founders in that place and I know a few, so this is really interesting. So you're roughly saying that maybe spend a year, year and a half on level one, which is you're just grinding, cold emailing, reaching out, selling customers, and maybe getting to five customers in the first year and a half. That's at the extreme, but that's a good outcome. And then maybe another year trying to get to... What was it? 20? 25 customers.
turns.zh: 有很多创业者都处于这种境地，我认识不少人，所以这真的很有意思。你的意思是，可能在第一阶段花一到一年半的时间，主要就是苦苦挣扎、发冷邮件、联系客户、销售产品，也许在第一年半就能获得五个客户。这是极端情况，但已经是个不错的结果。然后再花一年左右时间争取达到……多少个？20个？25个客户。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Going from five to 25 quickly. Yeah, if I see a company go from five customers to 25 in a year, that is almost always a sign that there's some pretty strong product-market fit there.
turns.zh: 从5个客户迅速增长到25个。是的，如果我看到一家公司在一年内从5个客户增长到25个，那几乎总是意味着产品与市场高度契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So many companies don't go through that, and they have the funding to keep iterating, exploring, trying to figure things out. I don't know if you have the answer here, but just what's your advice of if it's been four years and demand is not starting to come to them, they don't have 25 customers? Is it, "Wait until you run out of money, just give it a shot"? Or is it, "Let's just give the money back and move on to something else"?
turns.zh: 太棒了。很多公司没有经历这个过程，他们有资金支持不断迭代、探索、尝试理清思路。我不知道你对此有没有答案，但如果你已经四年了，需求还没开始涌现，没有25个客户，你会怎么做？是说“等资金用完了，再试试看”？还是说“把钱退回去，转向其他项目”？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Well, that's a personal decision for founders. I do think if you've been going at it for four to five years and you haven't started to find anything that you're really feeling pull from the market on, I don't know, you've done it for four to five years, what are the chances that you're going to magically find something? I think there are probably a handful of startups that do it that figure it out and get back on an amazing growth curve, but that's the exception rather than the rule. (01:10:46): So if a founder wants to return the money to investors, if a founder wants to look for a soft landing, there's no shame in that. Product-market fit is very, very hard. That's why we're doing this. It's why we're trying to increase the odds. And we're also trying to make it clear what it looks like and what it doesn't look like. And everybody knows when they do a startup that the odds are that you will not get there. So there's no shame in that, and I would completely be supportive of any founder who wants to take that path.
turns.zh: 嗯，这对创始人来说是个人的决定。我确实认为，如果你已经坚持了四到五年，却还没有开始从市场上感受到真正的需求吸引力——我不知道，你已经坚持了四到五年，还有多大机会能神奇地找到突破口呢？我认为可能只有少数几家初创公司能做到这一点，找到正确的方向并重回惊人的增长曲线，但这毕竟是例外而非规则。（01:10:46）：所以，如果创始人想把钱退给投资者，如果创始人想寻求一个软着陆的方案，这并不可耻。产品与市场的契合度非常、非常难。这就是我们做这项工作的原因。我们正努力提高成功概率，同时也努力清晰地界定成功与失败的标准。每个人都知道创业的成功概率很低。所以这并不可耻，我完全支持任何想走这条路的创始人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. I think that was a really important point to make. Let's quickly summarize the levels and then I want to also summarize the four Ps again, because I think that's the thing you can actually do. And so I think I just want to reinforce, "Here's the four things you should play with if things aren't going in the direction." So first of all, let's summarize the levels, what it looks like and what you should be focusing on there.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这条建议。我认为这是一个非常重要的观点。让我们快速总结一下各个阶段，然后我再再次总结一下四大要素，因为我认为这才是你真正能做的。所以我想强调一下，"如果事情没有朝着正确方向发展，以下四件事你应该尝试。"首先，让我们总结一下各个阶段的情况、它们的特征以及你应该关注的重点。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Okay. So level one, nascent product-market fit. You're just trying to get three to five customers and you're focused on satisfaction first and foremost. Level two is developing. This is where you're going from five to 25 customers, and you're really starting to focus on demand. Level three is strong product-market fit. You're going from 25 customers up to 100 or more, and you've got to start thinking about efficiency at that scale. And then level four is extreme, you're more than 100 customers, your company's awesome. You got to keep doing all three of those things well, and you have to start looking for ways to expand your total addressable market.
turns.zh: 好的。第一个阶段是产品与市场初步契合阶段。你只是在努力获得三到五个客户，首要关注的是客户满意度。第二个阶段是发展阶段。在这个阶段，你的客户数量从五个增加到25个，并且开始真正关注市场需求。第三个阶段是产品与市场强劲契合阶段。你的客户数量从25个增加到100个或更多，你需要开始考虑如何在这种规模下提高效率。然后第四个阶段是极致阶段，客户数量超过100个，你的公司非常出色。在这个阶段，你必须继续做好上述三件事，同时还要开始寻找方法来扩大你的潜在市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, perfect. And then let's come back to the four Ps. I have the draft. I have your post up here, so I have the detailed version of each of these things. But could you just talk through these four things? What is it you should be thinking about changing if things aren't working, the four Ps basically?
turns.zh: 好的，完美。然后再回到四大要素。我有初稿。我把你的帖子放在这里了，所以我有这些内容的详细版本。但你能否详细讲讲这四件事吗？如果事情没有顺利发展，你应该考虑改变什么，基本上就是这四大要素？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah. So the four Ps again are: persona, problem, promise, and product. And the persona is interesting because in some ways, it's synonymous with the market. A lot of people think of the market in this macroeconomic way where it's like, "Oh, it's this category of ERP software or whatever." I think it's much more tangible for a founder to think of the market as a collection of people. Jack Altman was thinking about his market as all of the HR leaders out there, and he was thinking about how many of them are there and what are the problems they have and how much money are they willing to spend on solving those problems. (01:13:12): It's a collection of people who have money to pay for a product or pay for a service. And so that's really the first piece, find the persona and really try to get into the mind of the persona. That's another thing I was amazed about spending time with Zach from Plaid, and Lloyd from Looker, and Jack from Lattice. They had all of these people, they were text messaging with all of their customers and they're meeting them on the weekends and stuff. They really, really knew their customer well. They were friends with their customers. (01:13:45): And so you've got to get so deep into the mind of the persona and: what are their challenges? What are their goals? How do you help them succeed at their job? That's the stuff that earns you the right to get the rest of the Ps right. And so the problem, obviously, comes next. And I think about this, and I can actually get into, Lenny, a little bit if you want to get into some of the customer discovery stuff because that's the second session.
turns.zh: 是的。所以四个P还是那些：人物、问题、承诺和产品。人物这部分很有意思，因为在某种程度上，它等同于市场。很多人把市场想得太宏观，比如“哦，这是ERP软件之类的品类”。但对于创业者来说，把市场看作是一群具体的人群要实在得多。杰克·奥特曼（Jack Altman）把他的市场定位为所有HR负责人，他研究了市场上到底有多少这样的高管，他们面临哪些挑战，愿意花多少钱来解决这些问题。（01:13:12）：市场就是一群有钱购买产品或服务的人群。这才是第一步——找到目标用户，真正理解他们的需求。最近我和Plaid的扎克（Zach）、Looker的劳埃德（Lloyd）以及Lattice的杰克（Jack）交流时，深切感受到他们对客户的了解。他们会和客户频繁发短信，周末见面沟通。他们真的非常了解自己的客户，跟客户成了朋友。（01:13:45）：所以你必须深入了解目标用户：他们面临哪些挑战？他们的目标是什么？如何帮助他们在工作中取得成功？只有做到这些，你才能有资格去处理后续的三个P。接下来自然是问题。关于这个问题，我可以稍微展开讲讲，伦尼（Lenny），如果你想深入探讨客户发现阶段的内容的话，因为这是第二个环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect segue.
turns.zh: 完美过渡。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: And I was talking a little bit about we think of it as dollar-driven customer discovery. And I think a lot of founders are familiar with customer discovery. I think they at least talk to customers, which is good. I don't think most of them do it in the highest signal way because again, the customers, they're people, they're nice, they're going to be polite. They're also not good at predicting things that they will use or buy or want. (01:14:41): They're very good at talking about their problems, but they're not necessarily good at predicting their own behavior. So we think about it in terms of dollar-driven discovery, which is how do you test the dollar potential of a hypothesis? And this is a whole two-hour session, but I'll try to do it briefly here just to give you a sense of it.
turns.zh: 我之前提到过，我们把客户发现视为以美元为导向的探索。我认为很多创业者都熟悉客户发现阶段。他们至少会和客户沟通，这很不错。但我觉得大多数人并没有采用最高效的方式，因为客户毕竟是人——他们友善、礼貌，但并不擅长预测自己会使用、购买或渴望什么样的产品。（01:14:41）：他们很善于谈论自己的问题，但不一定能准确预测自己的行为。所以我们从以美元为导向的探索角度出发，如何验证一个假设的商业潜力？这是一个整整两小时的课程，但我会尽量简要讲解，让大家有个概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, let's get into it. Let's keep going. I'm just joking.
turns.zh: 不，继续吧。开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: So you've got to identify extreme value. This is independent of what I'm building, Lenny. I want to hear about your problems and your challenges and what is most important to you. And so I need to do it in this non-leading way and I need to avoid the trap that we call happy years. Because I found a lot of founders, "I want to build this thing, I want you to like my thing." And so I look for the things that you say that support what I'm doing. That's the trap. And so I could just try it on you, Lenny. Yeah, I might say...
turns.zh: 所以你必须识别极端价值。这和我的项目无关，伦尼。我想听听你的问题、挑战，以及对你最重要的东西。我需要用一种不带引导性的方式去探寻，避免陷入“虚假共鸣”的陷阱。比如，我发现很多创业者会说：“我想开发这个产品，我希望你喜欢我的产品。”然后我就开始找能支持我观点的证据。这就是陷阱。我可以拿你来举例，伦尼。比如，我可能会说……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Okay, Lenny, so you're doing Lenny's Newsletter and you're building Lenny's Podcasts. When you think about we're sitting here in April, over the next three months, let's say, what are your top three goals for Lenny's Newsletter and Lenny's Podcast?
turns.zh: 好的，莱尼，你正在负责《莱尼通讯》和制作《莱尼播客》。现在是四月份，未来三个月里，你对《莱尼通讯》和《莱尼播客》有哪三个最重要的目标？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow, interesting. I'm trying to find a more scalable way to do this newsletter long-term. It's basically something I have to do for the rest of my life, in theory. I don't know if there's an exit path for this newsletter career, so I'm trying to find ways to scale this over time. That's one. Two is just up-leveling the quality of each podcast episode in terms of visuals and audio and trailers and things like that. And then three is make the community more valuable to everyone that listens that's in the newsletter community. Those are top of mind.
turns.zh: 哦，哇，真有意思。我正试图找到一种更可扩展的方式来长期运营这份通讯。理论上说，这份工作我得做一辈子。我不知道这份通讯事业是否有退出路径，所以我正想办法逐步提升其规模。这是第一个目标。第二个目标是提升每个播客集的质量，包括视觉效果、音频质量、预告片制作等方面的提升。第三个目标是让听众社区对所有订阅者更有价值。这些都是我当前最关注的方面。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Okay, awesome. And so what's hard about those three things? You said you want to scale the newsletter, you want to increase quality, you want to make the community awesome. What's hard about those things? Or what's standing in your way of doing those?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。那么这三个目标中哪部分最难实现呢？你说想扩大通讯规模、提升质量、增强社区价值。具体难点在哪？或者说阻碍你实现这些目标的因素是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't have the answer yet, I guess is the answer. I don't know exactly how to do this yet.
turns.zh: 我目前还没找到答案，我想这就是答案吧。我还不知道具体该怎么做。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: You don't know how to do it. Okay. It's probably a service in this case, not a product. What if I was able to give you a service that said, "Lenny, you're going to be able to scale this podcast. We are going to help you find the 500 best guests in the world that are really excellent. We're going to guarantee they show up. You're going to have endless content on your podcast, in your newsletter"? What do you think about that? What do you think about that idea?
turns.zh: 你不知道该怎么做。好的。这可能属于服务型项目，而非产品型。如果我能提供一项服务，告诉你：“莱尼，你能把播客规模做大了。我们会帮你找到全球500位最优秀的嘉宾，保证他们都能到场。你的播客和通讯内容将源源不断。”你觉得这个主意怎么样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd pay a lot of money for that.
turns.zh: 我愿意为此花大价钱。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Okay. So that's an example of a wow statement. And you probably had in the back of your mind, "How are you going to do that? Is that actually going to work?"
turns.zh: 好的，这就是一个令人惊叹的设想。你心里可能在想：“这怎么可能实现？真的能行吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: In my experience, that's a good thing and an exciting thing. If I'm pitching a product idea to somebody and they are like, "Wow, does that really work? And if that thing works, I'd sign up for the wait list today." That to me is like, "Okay, now I got to figure out how to build that thing, but I know if I am able to build it and deliver on that promise, they are going to want it." Or you would maybe say signs like you would demonstrate a behavior that shows that you're interested in. You'd be like, "Oh, Todd, can we meet again next week to talk about this?" Or like, "Hey Todd, I actually would love to show this to the people I work with. Can you send me the deck?" (01:18:06): Those are the signs that I'm looking for. If you had reacted like, "Yeah, that sounds kind of interesting," that's a no, right? That is a no. The word interesting is a polite way of saying no, right? And so I'm either looking for wow statements or I'm looking for demonstrated behavior that shows interest. I then would probably, if I want to keep going with this, and this is all in the identifying extreme value, I'd ask you, "Well, what stands out as valuable here to you?" And I want to hear you answer quickly. You mentioned it's either going to make my products so much better, it's going to drive success for my business, or it's going to save me a bunch of money or something. Save me a bunch of risk." But something where you would very quickly be able to identify why that's valuable to you. (01:18:51): So that part one is extreme value. Then I got to figure out ability to pay and willingness to pay. And for you, this is easy because you're not a 5,000 person company and you're the boss. So this is probably pretty streamlined. There's no procurement function at Lenny's Newsletter. So let's say I'm going after a bigger company. The questions I'd ask on confirming the ability to pay are: are you currently looking for a product like this? Or are you building something internally? (01:19:24): This is the Ironclad thing where Jason was like, "Oh, you're looking for a CLM already." Another way I think about it is if a customer has a problem, and I really think they have a problem, and they know they have the problem and they're looking for a solution for the problem. Or they've even tried to build their own solution to it and failed, that's the best customer. They want this thing badly. They've demonstrated that and they've actually failed at building it because they underestimated how hard it was. So are you currently looking for building a solution here?
turns.zh: 以我的经验来看，这是一件好事，也是令人兴奋的事。如果我向某人推销一个产品创意，他们会说：“哇，这真的能行吗？如果这个产品真能成功，我今天就想加入等待名单。” 对我来说，这意味着：“好吧，现在我得想办法把它做出来，但我知道如果我能成功开发并兑现承诺，他们肯定会想要它。” 或者你可能会看到一些迹象，比如对方表现出感兴趣的行为。比如：“哦，托德，我们下周能再见面讨论这个吗？” 或者“嘿，托德，我真的很想把这个展示给我的同事们。你能把演示文稿发给我吗？” （01:18:06）：这些就是我要寻找的信号。如果对方反应是“嗯，这听起来挺有趣的”，那就是拒绝，对吧？“有趣”其实是委婉的拒绝，对吧？所以我要么寻找令人惊叹的反馈，要么寻找显示出兴趣的行为。接下来如果我想继续推进（这都是在识别极高价值的过程里），我会问你：“嗯，对你来说，这里最有价值的是什么？” 我希望你能迅速回答。比如“这会让我的产品好很多”、“这会推动我的业务成功”、“这能为我节省一大笔钱”或者“这能降低我的风险”之类的。总之，你要能迅速指出这对你有何价值。  （01:18:51）：第一部分是识别极高价值。接下来我要确认支付能力和支付意愿。对你来说这很简单，因为你不是一家拥有 5000 名员工的大公司，而且你是老板。所以在 Lenny's Newsletter 这里可能比较简单。假设我要面对一家大公司。我确认支付能力时会问：你们现在是否在寻找这样的产品？或者你们内部是否正在开发类似产品？  （01:19:24）：这就是 Ironclad 提到的关键点。比如 Jason 说：“哦，你已经在找 CLM（客户生命周期管理）了。” 我也这么想：如果客户有问题，而且他们清楚自己有这个问题，并且正在寻找解决方案——或者他们甚至尝试过自己开发但失败了——那就是最理想的客户。他们迫切需要这个解决方案。他们已经证明了需求，却因为低估了难度而失败了。所以你现在是否也在寻找解决方案？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Essentially, there's a budget. You're looking for, "Is there money to go towards this problem"?
turns.zh: 本质上，就是要看预算。你的问题是：“有钱来解决这个问题吗？”

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: That's the next question I was going to say is where would a budget for this come from? And the best answer is that there's an existing budget. Either we already spend money in some way for a competing tool, or something that can be displaced by you, or we're spending, we put five engineers together to help build this thing. There's some source of budget that I can get. Then the question is, "Well, how does your team make decisions on third-party tools to bring on?" And you're never going to get the cleanest answer here. In larger companies, you might get semi-clean answers, but it's something like, "Okay, this manager can approve it directly up to a certain dollar amount. If not, it goes to this next level up of manager. And if we're going to spend more than 50K on it, we actually have to compare three different alternatives." (01:20:47): But whatever, there's some known process. That's what I'm looking for rather than just a bunch of ambiguity. So that's ability to pay. And then I'm going into willingness to pay. I don't want to try to quantify that. That's where I go, "What's your budget for solving this? What are you paying for this other tool? Let me show you mine. You think that you'd pay less for that or you'd pay more for that? Can you replace this other thing with the thing I have?" And then I love this question. I think you've had Madhavan Ramanujam on the show, right?
turns.zh: 接下来我想问的问题是，这笔预算从哪里来？最佳答案是，现有预算已经存在。要么我们已经在某种程度上为竞争产品花钱，要么有可以被你们替代的现有项目，又或者我们正在投入资源——比如组建五名工程师团队来开发这款产品。总之，我能找到资金来源。然后问题来了，“那么你们团队是如何决定引入第三方工具的？”对此你永远得不到一个清晰的答案。在大型企业里，你或许能得到相对明确的回复，但大多是这样的：“好的，这位经理可以直接批准不超过某个金额的申请。超过这个金额则需要上报给更高层级经理。如果预算超过5万美元，我们就必须对三个不同方案进行比较。”（01:20:47）不过无论如何，总归有某种既定流程。这才是我真正关心的——而不是一堆模糊不清的回答。所以先谈支付能力，再转向支付意愿。我不想试图量化这一点。我会问：“你们解决这个问题的预算是多少？你们为现有工具花了多少钱？让我给你们看看我的预算。你们觉得你们会为此支付更少或更多费用？能用我的方案替代现有工具吗？”我特别喜欢这个问题。我记得节目里请过马德哈万·拉马努贾姆（Madhavan Ramanujam），对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: He has this question, he's from Simon-Kucher. I love his thing of like, "Lenny, what is a fair price you would pay for this thing that I just described to you?" And then you say your thing. And then I go, "Okay. Well, what would be an expensive price?" And then I say, "Okay, what would be a prohibitively expensive price?" And you ask those three questions. And generally, when people tell you the fair price, it's a little bit of like they're trying to get a deal. And if the product's good, the expensive price is the one that they would actually pay. (01:21:47): Where they're saying it feels expensive, but you put it in front of them, and you say, "It costs this much," and if it's really good, they want it. And the prohibitively expensive one is the one that's too expensive and they'd have to just, "I just can't do that." So I love these style of questions. I think they're just a lot more specific than what I see most founders doing, which is just chatting with customers. You really want to try to put them to some questions where you know they're going to answer honestly because you're asking them questions. You're not asking them to speculate and you're asking them fairly concrete stuff. (01:22:18): Oh, and the thing I should say is it's a two-hour session, like I mentioned. It's one thing to explain this stuff, but it's another thing to see it. And so we show tons of Zoom recordings from founders who have gone through the program, and we actually do this thing where all the founders who are going through the program, they recorded all their videos, their customer discovery videos, and then our team watches all of the videos and creates highlight reels. (01:22:45): And we sit around in a room and watch them together and we say like, "Oh, look at these questions that Lenny asked. And did you see how the customer responded? Wow, that's an eyes-light-up moment." Or, "Todd asked these questions, he's leading the witness a little bit and the customer didn't seem that interested." So the thing that's interesting is as a founder, you never see anybody else's version of this. You only have your own experience. And so just seeing how other founders do this in a real live setting is super. People love it.
turns.zh: 他提出了这个问题，他来自西蒙-库彻咨询公司。我特别喜欢他提出的那种方式，比如：“莱尼，针对我刚刚向你描述的产品，你愿意支付多少钱？”然后你回答。接着我会说：“好，那什么样的价格算贵呢？”再问：“好，那什么样的价格算高得离谱呢？” 你需要连续问这三个问题。通常，当人们告诉你一个“公平价格”时，他们其实是在试图达成交易。如果产品质量不错，人们愿意支付的贵价才是他们真正愿意付出的价格。（01:21:47）：他们可能会说价格太高，但当你把价格摆在他们面前时，说：“这个价格就是这样。”如果产品确实优秀，他们就会想要购买。而高得离谱的价格则让人望而却步，根本无法接受。所以我特别喜欢这种提问方式。相比之下，大多数创业者只是和客户聊天，而这种方式要具体得多。你需要让他们回答真实的问题，而不是让他们猜测。你要问他们具体的问题，让他们知道你在认真倾听他们的回答。（01:22:18）：哦，我还得说明一下，这是一次两小时的课程。光是讲解这些方法还不够，关键在于实践。我们展示了许多参与过该项目的创业者的Zoom录像。我们会把所有创业者的客户发现视频都收集起来，然后团队会剪辑成精彩片段。（01:22:45）：我们一起观看这些视频，评论道：“看看莱尼问的这些问题，客户的反应真是太棒了。” 或者：“托德问这些问题时，明显在引导客户，客户似乎不太感兴趣。” 有趣的是，作为创业者，你永远无法看到别人的做法，只能根据自己的经验判断。因此，亲眼目睹其他创业者在真实场景中的表现真是太棒了。大家都很喜欢这种方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's always easy to hear these things. It's much harder to be the person asking these questions to a potential customer you're trying to sell. And it's just asking, "How much would you pay for this?" So I love that you kind of force people through the actual practice of it. Todd, you're going to get a lot of applicants for this program. This sounds amazing. I know you're giving a peek at the stuff that we haven't really talked about. On this point you just shared, which is essentially trying to get real skin in the game insight into how big of a problem this is, I love that you just basically shared a bunch of questions. (01:23:43): Someone could just rewind right now and just write down all these questions that you shared and use them when you're talking to customers. Obviously, the classic problem is they tell you they're going to buy it but they don't. And all the stuff you shared is, "Here's ways to get at: will they actually buy it before they have the actual product?" Is there anything else you want to say on that? Just tips for not being tricked and people just saying, "Oh, yeah, I love this thing"? I know you talked through a lot of this, but anything else?
turns.zh: 这些方法听起来容易，但要亲自向潜在客户提出这些问题却很难。比如“你愿意为这个产品付多少钱？”所以我很欣赏你让人们亲自实践这些技巧。托德，你的这个项目肯定会吸引很多申请者。听起来太棒了。我知道你已经透露了一些我们还没谈到的内容。就你刚刚分享的这个要点——深入了解客户需求，判断他们是否真正有需求——我特别喜欢你分享的这些问题。（01:23:43）：现在听众可以倒回去，把你分享的这些问题都记下来，用于和客户沟通。显然，常见的问题是客户说要买，但实际没买。你分享的所有方法都是为了在产品真正推出前，就判断他们是否会购买。关于这个问题，你还有什么想补充的吗？比如如何避免被客户忽悠，或者他们只是说说而已？我知道你已经讲了很多，但还有什么要补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a couple of things. One is you have to know what to show people when you're actually showing them something. Lattice is the kind of product I mentioned that could be sold with Figma mock-ups. Looker couldn't be sold that way. Looker, you actually had to do a demo with their real data. So it required a lot more work to do that. Vanta was neither like a demo or a mock-up, it was actually doing the work. And Pilot was like that. There's a bunch of companies like that. So you have to figure out what is my product and how does it solve the problem? And therefore, what fidelity does my early product or early demo have to be at in order to land the sale? (01:24:44): And then I think you have to know when you've talked to enough people. It takes time to talk to people. And the rule of thumb is if you talk to enough people and you can predict 70 to 80% of what the next person is going to say to you, because you've just talked to so many people and you've heard the pattern so clearly, that's when you've talked to enough people. But these are all things you got to learn. And that's why doing it experientially in the way that we do the program we think was best.
turns.zh:
是的，我认为有几个关键点。首先，你必须清楚在实际向客户展示产品时，该展示什么内容。比如，我提到的Lattice产品，就可以用Figma的模型演示来推销，但Looker却不行，因为它需要用真实数据进行演示，这就需要投入更多精力。Vanta既不是演示也不是模型，而是实际的开发工作。Pilot也是如此。还有很多类似的公司。所以你必须明确自己的产品是什么，如何解决客户痛点？因此，早期产品或演示需要达到怎样的真实度才能促成交易？（01:24:44）  

接下来，我认为你还需要判断与多少潜在客户交流过才算足够。这需要花时间去沟通。经验法则是，如果你与足够多的人交流后，能预测到下一个人会说什么内容的70%到80%，这就意味着你已经与足够多的人沟通过了。但这些都是需要亲身实践才能掌握的技能。这也是我们为什么认为我们的项目采用实践教学模式最为有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that we haven't covered that you wanted to touch on before we let you go?
turns.zh: 有没有我们没有涉及到但你想在结束前提及的内容？

turns.en: No. If you're listening, if you're a B2B founder in those early days of starting your company, or you know anyone who fits that description, and you have an appreciation for just how hard it is to find product-market fit and you don't want to go it alone, then please apply to this program or share the application. Like we promise, we will review every single application. And I'm just really looking forward to working with a group of 20 or so amazing founders, and helping them navigate these early days of product-market fit finding. It's what I love to do.
turns.zh: 没有。如果你正在听讲座，或者你认识任何处于创业初期阶段的B2B创始人，并且你深知寻找产品-市场匹配的难度有多大，又不想独自面对挑战，那么请申请这个项目，或者分享申请链接。我们承诺会仔细审核每一份申请。我非常期待与20位左右优秀的创始人合作，帮助他们度过产品-市场匹配的初期阶段。这正是我热爱做的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to make sure the right people apply, remind people who is a great fit. So it's B2B founders, and you said they've been at it for six to nine months, something like that?
turns.zh: 为了确保合适的人申请，请提醒大家谁最适合这个项目。你说的是B2B创始人，他们创立公司的时间在6到9个月左右？

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: Yeah, something in that zone or earlier. You have an idea of what your product is. You have a hypothesis about what it is and who it's for, but you probably haven't started writing any code yet.
turns.zh: 是的，在这一阶段或更早阶段。他们对自己的产品有初步想法，对目标客户有假设，但可能还没有开始写代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if they've been at it for four years and haven't found success, this is not a fit.
turns.zh: 如果他们已经尝试了四年但仍未取得成功，那就不适合这个项目了。

turns.speaker: Todd Jackson
turns.en: I could try to help them one-on-one, but no, that's not a fit for this program.
turns.zh: 我可以尝试一对一帮助他们，但不适合这个项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how do they apply and when are their applications due?
turns.zh: 那么如何申请？申请截止日期是什么时候？

And yeah, I'm looking forward to working with some amazing founders that I know are listening right now.
turns.zh: 是的。请访问pmf.firstround.com。申请通道已开放，将持续至5月7日，项目将于5月29日正式启动。如果你想直接联系我，可以在Twitter上找到我，账号是@tjack。我会回复DM。期待与现在正在听讲座的优秀创始人合作。

turns.en: Amazing. I'm so happy we did this. I feel like this conversation is going to help a ton of founders, and they're going to come back to it again and again. Todd, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。很高兴我们能举办这次对话。我相信这次交流将帮助许多创始人，他们会反复回味这段内容。Todd，非常感谢你的参与。
